Integration by parts gives [xeˣ]₀¹−∫₀¹eˣdx=e−(e−1)=1. The choice simplifies the polynomial factor under differentiation. For area between a curve and the x-axis, split intervals at sign changes and integrate absolute contributions; the integral of x on [−1,1] is zero but geometric area is 1. An improper integral such as ∫₁∞1/x²dx is a limit: ∫₁ᴹ1/x²dx=1−1/M tends to 1. ∫₁∞1/x dx instead grows as ln M and diverges; formally writing an antiderivative is not proof of convergence.

gateGuide.recognize: Decide whether the problem asks signed integral or geometric area. For substitutions and improper endpoints, keep the transformed variable and limits explicit.
method: Choose a simplification: elementary antiderivative, substitution, integration by parts or symmetry. State why its conditions apply.
Write an antiderivative or transformed integral on its own line; change both limits if using a new variable.
Evaluate upper minus lower, inspect signs and units, and use actual one-sided limits at singularities or infinity.

traps.claim: Signed integral is always area
traps.why: The integral of x from −1 to 1 is zero, but geometric area is 1 because negative and positive areas both count positively.

traps.claim: Symmetry resolves a singular integral
traps.why: The ordinary improper integral of 1/x from −1 to 1 does not exist. A symmetric principal value is a different definition and cannot be silently substituted.

formulas.meaning: For an appropriate antiderivative and a well-defined integral.
Integration by parts.
Check integrability before using cancellation.

lessons.title: Probability, conditional probability and Bayes
lessons.intuition: A conditional probability changes the population under consideration. Once B is known, count only outcomes inside B. Bayes reverses a conditioning direction by combining prior frequencies with evidence; a high detection rate need not imply a high probability that a detected condition is real.

sections.title: Events and conditioning
sections.body: A probability measure assigns nonnegative values totaling 1 to the sample space. For P(B)>0, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). The multiplication rule gives P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B). Mutually exclusive nonzero-probability events cannot be independent, because their intersection is empty.

sections.title: Total probability and Bayes
sections.body: If B₁,…,Bₖ form a partition, P(A)=ΣP(A|Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ). Bayes gives P(Bⱼ|A)=P(A|Bⱼ)P(Bⱼ)/P(A). Construct the denominator from every way the evidence can occur. Use a frequency table when fractions feel abstract: population counts often make false positives obvious.

sections.title: Independence
sections.body: A and B are independent iff P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A|B)=P(A) when defined. Pairwise independence among three events is weaker than mutual independence: the triple intersection must also factor. Do not infer independence from different-looking descriptions.

sections.title: A table prevents reversed conditioning
sections.body: Use rows for cause classes and columns for evidence outcomes. For prevalence 0.2, sensitivity 0.8 and false-positive rate 0.1, among 1000 cases there are 200 positives-by-condition, of which 160 test positive; among the 800 without the condition, 80 test positive. Hence P(test positive)=240/1000 and P(condition|test positive)=160/240=2/3. The denominator is everyone with the evidence, not everyone with the condition. The formula agrees: 0.8×0.2/[0.8×0.2+0.1×0.8]. Independence can also be tested by checking whether conditioning leaves the probability unchanged. Sampling without replacement often destroys that equality because the first draw changes the remaining population.

examples.prompt: A test has sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 10%, and prevalence 1%. Find \(P(\text{condition}\mid\text{positive})\)

steps.title: Label events and joint probabilities
steps.explanation: D means having the condition. Sensitivity is P(+|D), not the posterior probability being asked for.

steps.title: Count positives without the condition
steps.explanation: The large noncondition population can contribute more positives despite its smaller per-person positive rate.

steps.title: Normalize within all positives
steps.explanation: The denominator is total positive probability. Omitting false positives or the prevalence changes the event being computed.

examples.given: Prevalence 0.01; sensitivity 0.90; false-positive rate 0.10.
examples.goal: Find the probability of the condition given a positive test.
examples.strategy: Account for both sources of positive tests, then restrict to the positive population.
examples.answer: Approximately 8.33%.
examples.verification: Among 10,000 people: 90 true positives and 990 false positives; 90/1080 reproduces the posterior.

examples.prompt: Draw two cards without replacement; find probability both are aces

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: A₁ is an ace on the first draw. The standard deck has four aces among 52 cards.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: Conditioned on an ace already being removed, three aces remain among 51 cards. The draws are not independent.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: The multiplication rule uses a conditional second factor. Reusing 4/52 would silently change the experiment to replacement.

examples.strategy: Multiply a marginal probability by the correct conditional probability.
examples.answer: Multiply \(\frac4{52}\frac3{51}=\frac1{221}\). Treating the draws as independent would use the wrong second factor.
examples.verification: An unordered count gives C(4,2)/C(52,2)=6/1326=1/221, agreeing with the sequential calculation.

pitfalls: P(A|B) is usually not P(B|A).
Disjointness and independence are different.

checks.prompt: Two disjoint events each have positive probability. Are they independent?
checks.hint: Compare zero intersection with the product of positive probabilities.
checks.explanation: Their intersection probability is zero while P(A)P(B)>0, violating independence.
options: Only because their intersection is zero
Cannot be determined even with disjointness

checks.prompt: Independent events have probabilities 0.2 and 0.5. What is their intersection probability?
checks.hint: Multiply independent probabilities.

gateGuide.recognize: Conditioning changes the denominator. Disease tests, manufacturing sources and urn selections become clearer when all ways to obtain the observed evidence are counted.
method: Define the cause classes and write their priors; state which event is already known.
Compute evidence probability by total probability across every class, including false positives or alternative sources.
Use Bayes to reverse the condition. Check that posterior is between zero and one and that plausible evidence changes the prior in the expected direction.

traps.claim: High sensitivity gives high posterior
traps.why: With a rare condition, false positives among the much larger healthy group can outnumber true positives. Posterior also depends on prevalence.

traps.claim: Using independent probabilities without justification
traps.why: Two draws without replacement change the population; the second factor must be conditional on the first.

formulas.meaning: Conditional probability restricts the sample population to B.
Bayes with a partition of possible causes.
Disjointness is not independence.

lessons.title: Random variables and descriptive statistics
lessons.intuition: A random variable attaches a number to an outcome. The distribution tells you how often values occur; expectation, variance, and quantiles summarize different aspects. An average alone cannot tell you whether values are tightly concentrated or widely spread.

sections.title: PMF, PDF and CDF
sections.body: For discrete X, p(x)=P(X=x) is a probability mass function and its values sum to 1. For continuous X, a density f integrates to 1; probabilities are areas, so P(X=x)=0 at individual points. The cumulative distribution F(x)=P(X≤x) works in both cases and is nondecreasing.

sections.title: Expectation and dispersion
sections.body: For discrete X, \(E[X]\)=Σxp(x); for continuous X, integrate xf(x). E[aX+b]=a\(E[X]\)+b without needing independence. Var(X)=\(E[X^2]\)−\(E[X]\)² and Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X). Standard deviation is the square root of variance. Variances of sums add for independent variables; otherwise covariance terms matter.

sections.title: Mean, median and mode
sections.body: The arithmetic mean uses every observation and is sensitive to outliers. Median splits the ordered data into halves and resists extreme values. Mode is a most frequent value and need not be unique. Distinguish population variance, with divisor n, from the conventional unbiased sample variance, with divisor n−1, when the question specifies a sample estimator.

sections.title: Deriving variance and using linearity
sections.body: Variance is E[(X−μ)²], where μ=\(E[X]\). Expand the square: E[X²−2μX+μ²]=\(E[X^2]\)−2μ\(E[X]\)+μ²=\(E[X^2]\)−μ². This explains why the second moment, not just the mean, is needed. For a count X=I₁+…+Iₙ of indicator variables, \(E[X]\)=ΣE[Iᵢ]=ΣP(Iᵢ=1), even when the events are dependent. Variance addition requires checking covariance: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Independent variables have covariance zero, but zero covariance alone does not establish independence in general. Scaling all observations by 3 scales deviations by 3 and squared deviations by 9, while adding a constant leaves deviations unchanged.

examples.prompt: Compute moments when X is 0 or 2 with equal probability

steps.title: Compute the mean
steps.explanation: Expectation is the probability-weighted value, which need not itself be a possible outcome.

steps.title: Compute the second moment
steps.explanation: Square each outcome before averaging. Squaring the mean would instead give 1 and is not the second moment.

steps.title: Compute spread
steps.explanation: Variance is in squared units; standard deviation is the nonnegative square root in the original units.

examples.given: X takes 0 and 2, each with probability 1/2.
examples.goal: Find mean, variance and standard deviation.
examples.strategy: Compute first and second moments separately, then subtract the squared first moment.
examples.answer: Mean 1, variance 1, standard deviation 1.
examples.verification: The deviations from mean are −1 and +1, so their squared values are both 1; their weighted average confirms variance 1.

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: The mean includes every observation, so the large final value has considerable influence.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: For five sorted observations the third is the median. The value two also has the largest occurrence count.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: The difference between mean and median signals this sample’s right-skewed extreme observation; the statistics need not coincide.

examples.strategy: Calculate mean, median and mode according to their distinct definitions.
examples.answer: The large observation shifts the mean away from the typical central values.
examples.verification: Removing 12 changes the mean to 2 while the central repeated values remain near 2, illustrating the mean’s sensitivity.

pitfalls: A PDF value is a density, not a point probability.
\(E[X^2]\) is not generally \(E[X]\)².

checks.prompt: For continuous X with a density, what is P(X=c) at an individual point?
checks.hint: A single point has zero interval width.
checks.explanation: Continuous point probability is zero; interval probability is an integral of density, not a density value.

checks.prompt: If Var(X)=4, what is Var(3X+7)?
checks.hint: A shift does not affect variance.

gateGuide.recognize: Moment questions distinguish E[X²] from E[X]². Continuous-density questions require normalization before expectation or interval probability.
method: Check the PMF sums or PDF integrates to one; solve any unknown normalization constant first.
Compute first and second moments separately, then variance. For transformed variables use linearity and the square scaling rule.
For data summaries sort before finding median, and check whether the variance requested is population or an unbiased sample estimator.

traps.claim: E[X²]=E[X]²
traps.why: For a fair variable taking 0 or 2, these are 2 and 1 respectively. Their difference is the nonzero variance.

traps.claim: Adding a constant changes variance
traps.why: It shifts all values and the mean equally, so deviations are unchanged. Scaling by a multiplies variance by a², even if a is negative.

formulas.meaning: Discrete first and second moments.
Variance is never negative for a valid distribution.
Translations leave spread unchanged.

lessons.title: Binomial and Poisson distributions
lessons.intuition: The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent identical trials. Poisson models event counts in a window with a specified mean rate. Identify the experiment first: fixed trials and success probability suggest binomial; an event rate over time suggests Poisson.

sections.title: Binomial construction
sections.body: X~Binomial(n,p) has P(X=k)=C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. The combination chooses success positions; multiplying gives the probability of a specific ordering. \(E[X]\)=np and Var(X)=np(1−p). At least one success is conveniently 1−(1−p)ⁿ.

sections.title: Poisson counts
sections.body: X~Poisson(λ) has P(X=k)=e^(−λ)λᵏ/k!, k≥0. Its mean and variance are both λ. If the rate is r per unit time, a duration t has λ=rt under the homogeneous Poisson-process model. Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count with summed means.

sections.title: When approximation is sensible
sections.body: For many independent trials with small p and moderate np, Binomial(n,p) can be approximated by Poisson(np). It is an approximation, not a rule replacing all binomial questions. Check the event and units; changing a 1-minute window to 3 minutes multiplies λ by three, not p by three.

sections.title: Deriving binomial moments with indicators
sections.body: Write the success count X as the sum of n independent Bernoulli indicators Iᵢ. Each has mean p and variance p(1−p), so expectation is np and independent variances sum to np(1−p). The mass formula contains C(n,k) because there are that many ways to place k successes among n positions. For Poisson with rate 3/hour, a 20-minute interval has λ=1, not λ=3: converting the window is part of specifying the distribution. Then P(exactly two)=e⁻¹/2. A binomial n=1000,p=0.001 has mean 1; its zero-count probability (0.999)^1000 is close to e⁻¹, illustrating the rare-event approximation without treating it as an exact equality.

examples.prompt: Fair coin tossed four times: exactly two heads

steps.title: Identify the model
steps.explanation: There are a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same head probability. These assumptions justify the binomial model.

steps.title: Count successful sequences
steps.explanation: Choose the two head positions; order of choosing these positions does not matter.

steps.title: Weight each sequence
steps.explanation: Each length-four sequence has probability 1/16. The six sequences are disjoint, so add their probabilities.

examples.given: Four independent fair coin tosses; exactly two heads required.
examples.goal: Find the probability.
examples.strategy: Count valid head positions and multiply by the probability of each disjoint ordering.
examples.verification: The five binomial counts are 1,4,6,4,1; summing gives 16 equally likely outcomes.

examples.prompt: Calls arrive with rate 2 per minute. Find mean and zero-call probability in 3 minutes

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: The Poisson model parameter is expected events over the entire interval, not the per-minute rate by itself.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: For a Poisson count, both mean and variance equal its parameter. Standard deviation is √6, not six.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: At zero, both the power and factorial equal one. The resulting probability is about 0.00248 under the homogeneous Poisson assumptions.

examples.strategy: Convert the rate into a mean for the stated time window before using the PMF.
examples.answer: \(P(X=0)=e^{-6}\frac{6^0}{0!}=e^{-6}\); the duration must be included before using the formula.
examples.verification: A longer interval has a larger mean and a smaller no-event probability; using e⁻² would describe one minute rather than three.

pitfalls: Binomial trials need the same p and independence.
Poisson λ belongs to the actual time window.

checks.prompt: Which experiment directly fits a binomial model?
checks.hint: Identify fixed trials, independence and a common p.
checks.explanation: Binomial counts successes under those three assumptions. A rate-based event count may instead use Poisson, and waiting time may be continuous.
options: A fixed number of independent equal-probability success/failure trials
A continuous value uniformly sampled from an interval

checks.prompt: A Poisson process has rate 4 per hour. What is the count variance over 2 hours?
checks.hint: Compute the window mean first.
checks.explanation: λ=4×2=8; Poisson variance equals λ.

lessons.example: Fair coin tossed four times: exactly two heads

gateGuide.recognize: Match the experiment to the distribution: fixed independent equal-p trials for binomial; event counts with a specified window rate for Poisson.
method: Write n,p or the actual window mean λ before plugging in a mass formula.
For at least one event, compute one minus zero instead of summing every positive count.
For independent counts use indicators or distribution addition, but treat Poisson approximation as an approximation and retain the correct time-unit conversion.

traps.claim: Poisson rate equals mean for every window
traps.why: A rate of 6 per hour has mean 2 in 20 minutes. The rate must be multiplied by the duration in consistent units.

traps.claim: Any sequence of trials is binomial
traps.why: Changing success probabilities or dependence invalidates the elementary binomial model even when outcomes are successes/failures.

formulas.meaning: Binomial mass for k=0,…,n.
Binomial moments.
Poisson mass with mean/variance λ for a duration t.

lessons.title: Uniform, exponential and normal distributions
lessons.intuition: Continuous probabilities are interval areas. Uniform gives equal density over a bounded interval; exponential models waiting time with a constant hazard; normal describes symmetric variation around a mean. Each has a different support and interpretation.

sections.title: Uniform[a,b]
sections.body: The density is 1/(b−a) inside [a,b] and zero outside. An interval probability is its overlapping length divided by b−a. Mean=(a+b)/2 and variance=(b−a)²/12. Equal density does not mean a positive probability at each exact point; any one point still has probability zero.

sections.title: Exponential rate λ
sections.body: The density is λe^(−λx) for x≥0; survival P(X>t)=e^(−λt). Mean=1/λ and variance=1/λ². Memorylessness follows because P(X>s+t|X>s)=e^(−λ(s+t))/e^(−λs)=e^(−λt). The rate parameter is the reciprocal of the mean, so check which parameterization the question uses.

sections.title: Normal(μ,σ²)
sections.body: The density is symmetric around μ, so mean=median=mode=μ. Standardize using Z=(X−μ)/σ, not σ². Probabilities reduce to standard normal CDF Φ: P(a<X<b)=Φ((b−μ)/σ)−Φ((a−μ)/σ). Independent normal variables have normal sums with means and variances added.

sections.title: Normalize a density before calculating probabilities
sections.body: If f(x)=cx on [0,2] and zero outside, normalization requires ∫₀²cx dx=2c=1, so c=1/2. Then P(1<X<2)=∫₁²x/2 dx=3/4, and \(E[X]\)=∫₀²x²/2 dx=4/3. This distribution is not uniform because density grows with x. For exponential waiting time, conditional survival divides two survival probabilities and cancels the elapsed factor, explaining memorylessness directly. For normal variables, convert an interval using standard deviation before looking up Φ. If Y=aX+b for a negative a, inequality direction reverses when standardizing an event; keeping the event itself visible avoids sign errors.

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: Uniform density normalizes the total area across the six-unit support to one.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: Both event bounds lie inside the support; otherwise first intersect with [2,8]. A density value is not itself an interval probability.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: Multiply constant density by interval length. Strict versus non-strict endpoints do not change a continuous distribution’s interval probability.

examples.strategy: Integrate constant density over the part of the support that satisfies the event.
examples.answer: Probability=2/6=1/3; the density 1/6 alone is not the answer.
examples.verification: The event spans two of the support’s six units, so its probability must be 2/6. The entire support has probability 6/6=1.

steps.title: Extract standard deviation
steps.explanation: The second parameter is variance, so taking the square root is necessary. A paper using Normal(mean,standard deviation) must explicitly be treated differently.

steps.title: Standardize the boundary
steps.explanation: Subtract the center and divide by the scale. Dividing by variance would give the wrong number of standard deviations.

steps.title: Translate the event
steps.explanation: The scale is positive, so the inequality direction stays the same. Φ denotes the standard-normal CDF; use a supplied table when a numeric approximation is requested.

examples.given: \(X\sim N(10,4)\), using the convention Normal(mean,variance).
examples.goal: Standardize x=14 and express its cumulative probability.
examples.strategy: Read the parameter convention before converting to a standard normal variable.
examples.answer: \(z=2\), and cumulative probability \(\Phi(2)\).
examples.verification: 14 is four units above the mean, which is exactly two standard deviations of two units each.

pitfalls: Normal notation typically gives variance, not standard deviation.
Exponential rate and scale are reciprocals.

checks.prompt: For Normal(μ,σ²), which standardization is correct?
checks.hint: Divide by standard deviation, not variance.
checks.explanation: Z=(X−μ)/σ centers by the mean and scales by standard deviation.

checks.prompt: An exponential distribution has rate 0.25 per minute. What is its mean waiting time in minutes?
checks.hint: Mean is reciprocal rate.
checks.explanation: 1/0.25=4 minutes.

gateGuide.recognize: Read whether a parameter is rate, variance or standard deviation. Continuous probabilities concern intervals rather than density heights.
method: Identify support and parameterization, then choose CDF/survival, interval fraction or normal standardization.
Transform event bounds as well as variables. If a scale factor is negative, reverse the inequality.
Inspect edge cases: probabilities outside support, symmetric normal half-probabilities, and the reciprocal relation between exponential rate and mean.

traps.claim: Dividing by normal variance
traps.why: Normal(10,4) has σ=2, so X=14 standardizes to 2, not 1.

traps.claim: Density is a point probability
traps.why: A uniform density can be greater than 1 on a short interval while all probabilities remain at most 1. Integrating over an interval gives probability.

formulas.meaning: Uniform[a,b] probability includes support overlap.
Exponential with rate λ and t≥0.
Normal standardization uses standard deviation.

name: Digital Logic
description: From Boolean expressions to working circuits

lessons.title: Boolean algebra and algebraic minimization
lessons.intuition: Boolean simplification preserves a function while reducing the gates required to implement it. Work with identities valid for every input. Boolean addition is OR, so 1+1=1; ordinary numerical cancellation cannot be imported without checking it.

sections.title: Basic identities
sections.body: Identity laws give A+0=A and A·1=A; domination gives A+1=1 and A·0=0. Complement gives A+¬A=1 and A¬A=0. Idempotence gives A+A=A and AA=A. Absorption A+AB=A removes a redundant condition. De Morgan moves negation through a gate and swaps AND with OR.

sections.title: Canonical forms
sections.body: A minterm specifies every variable and is true on exactly one truth-table row. Sum the minterms where the function is 1 to obtain canonical SOP. A maxterm is false on exactly one row; multiply maxterms for rows where the function is 0 to obtain canonical POS. Ordinary simplified SOP need not contain every variable in every term.

sections.title: Simplifying systematically
sections.body: Combine terms differing in only one literal: AB+A¬B=\(A(B+\overline B)=A\). Remove absorbed terms and apply the consensus rule XY+¬XZ+YZ=XY+¬XZ. Confirm the result with a truth table when unsure. Fewer literals and fewer gates are related but distinct implementation cost measures.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Factor the first two terms: \(A(B+\overline B)=A\). Complementarity makes B+¬B=1 for either Boolean B; multiplication by A then leaves A.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Now \(F=A+AC\). The removed terms together cover every case where A is true. Keep the remaining AC term until absorption is justified.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Absorption removes AC, leaving F=A for all inputs. When A=0, both terms are zero; when A=1, the first term already forces output one. Thus C cannot change the result.

examples.strategy: Use a Boolean identity at each transformation, rather than ordinary arithmetic.
examples.answer: Absorption removes AC, leaving F=A for all inputs.
examples.verification: Try A=0 and A=1 with both C values; the output always equals A. Boolean + is OR, so 1+1=1 here.

examples.prompt: Build SOP for a 2-variable function true on 01 and 11
steps: The corresponding minterms are ¬AB and AB.
\(F=\overline AB+AB=B(\overline A+A)\).
The simplified expression is B, so the output ignores A.

pitfalls: Boolean OR is not arithmetic addition.
A canonical term must contain every variable.

checks.prompt: Which algebraic law explains A+AB=A?
checks.hint: The second term is already contained in the first condition.
checks.explanation: Absorption removes AB because whenever AB is true, A is already true; it adds no new accepting assignments.

checks.prompt: How many input assignments make F=A true in a 3-variable function A,B,C?
checks.hint: B and C remain unconstrained.
checks.explanation: Fix A=1; B and C each have 2 choices, yielding 4.

method: Expand or factor with Boolean identities, not ordinary subtraction. Establish whether SOP or POS is requested.
Use absorption and complement pairs before expanding everything; fewer terms often expose the essential variable.
Check the simplified form on a discriminating assignment, especially rows where eliminated literals change.

traps.claim: Using arithmetic cancellation
traps.why: A+A=A, not 2A. Likewise A+AB=A because AB adds no accepting row beyond A.

traps.claim: Minimal and canonical mean the same
traps.why: A canonical minterm names every variable; a minimal implicant intentionally omits changing variables.

formulas.meaning: Absorption and combining complementary cases.
De Morgan swaps AND and OR.

lessons.title: Karnaugh maps and the tabular method
lessons.intuition: Adjacent minterms differ in one variable, so combining them eliminates that variable. Karnaugh maps make this adjacency visual; the tabular method performs the same operation symbolically and scales without relying on a drawing.

sections.title: K-map layout and grouping
sections.body: Use Gray-code labels such as 00,01,11,10 so neighbours differ in one bit. Group 1s in rectangles with 1,2,4,8,… cells. Edges wrap around and corners may be adjacent; diagonal cells are not adjacent. A group with 2ᵏ cells eliminates k variables. Overlap is allowed and often necessary; every required 1 must be covered.

sections.title: Prime and essential implicants
sections.body: A prime implicant cannot be enlarged into another valid group. An essential prime implicant covers a minterm covered by no other prime implicant and must be selected. After selecting essentials, cover remaining minterms with a low-cost collection. Don’t-care cells may be included as 1s to enlarge a group or ignored; there is no requirement to cover them.

sections.title: Quine–McCluskey
sections.body: Write minterms in binary, group by number of 1s, and combine terms differing in one specified bit, replacing that bit by a dash. Repeat until no more combinations are possible. Uncombined terms are prime implicants. Build a chart mapping primes to covered required minterms and select a cover. This separates implicant generation from the covering problem.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The minterms are 000,001,010,011. Use ABC bit order consistently: changing the assumed variable order changes the resulting literal.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Across the four-cell group B and C take both values but A stays 0. The group is a complete power-of-two block, so all four B,C combinations are represented. A varying literal is unnecessary.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Eliminate B,C to get \(F=\overline A\). The literal is complemented because the retained A bit is zero, not one.

examples.strategy: Enumerate binary minterms and retain only literals constant across the group.
examples.answer: Eliminate B,C to get \(F=\overline A\).
examples.verification: ¬A is true exactly for minterms 0 through 3, and false for minterms 4 through 7; this checks the entire truth table.

steps: They differ only in the final bit.
Replace that position by a dash: 101−.
For variables A,B,C,D the product is \(A\overline BC\); D is eliminated.

pitfalls: K-map labels use Gray order, not binary numeric order.
Larger groups should not include required zero cells.
revision: Essential implicants cover uniquely covered required minterms.

checks.prompt: Which K-map grouping is allowed?
checks.hint: Logical adjacency differs from ordinary diagram distance.
checks.explanation: Valid groups are rectangular powers of two in Gray-code adjacency, with wraparound allowed. Required zero cells cannot be used.
options: A power-of-two rectangle that can wrap around edges
A group containing a required zero

checks.prompt: How many differing specified bits may be combined in one Quine–McCluskey step?
checks.hint: Combining removes one bit position.
checks.explanation: Exactly one differing specified bit is replaced by a dash.

traps.claim: Diagonal cells are adjacent
traps.why: A diagonal can change two input bits, so combining it does not eliminate just one literal.

traps.claim: All don’t-cares must be covered
traps.why: They represent unconstrained outputs. Covering unnecessary ones can make the implementation larger instead of smaller.

formulas.meaning: A group of g=2^k cells in an n-variable map eliminates k changing variables.

lessons.title: Designing combinational circuits
lessons.intuition: A combinational circuit has no memory: outputs are determined by current inputs. The design process starts with a behavioural specification, translates it to a truth table, simplifies the output equations, and maps them to available gates or modules.

sections.title: Adders and arithmetic building blocks
sections.body: A half adder produces sum A⊕B and carry AB. A full adder includes Cin: sum=A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout=AB+ACin+BCin. Cascading full adders yields a ripple-carry adder whose worst delay grows with the carry path length. A carry-lookahead adder uses generate G=AB and propagate P=A⊕B to compute carry dependencies more directly.

sections.title: Multiplexers and decoders
sections.body: A 2ᵏ:1 multiplexer selects one of 2ᵏ data inputs using k select bits. A decoder maps k inputs to up to 2ᵏ one-hot outputs. Implement a Boolean function with a mux by assigning select variables, then making each data input the residual function of remaining variables. Decoder minterm outputs can be ORed for SOP implementation.

sections.title: Design and timing
sections.body: Validate all input combinations, including active-high/active-low control conventions. Gates have propagation delays; the longest input-to-output path determines worst-case settling. Logical equivalence alone does not remove hazards caused by unequal physical path delays. Combinational feedback without carefully defined storage is not ordinary combinational design.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: \(S=1\oplus1\oplus0=0\). XOR represents addition modulo two, so the sum bit records the parity of the three inputs.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: \(C_{out}=AB+AC_{in}+BC_{in}=1+0+0=1\). Each product tests one pair of high inputs. OR of these products is one precisely when at least two inputs are high.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The pair Cout,S represents binary 10, correctly summing decimal 2. Carry is the higher-weight bit; reversing the pair would incorrectly turn decimal two into one.

examples.strategy: Evaluate sum and carry independently, then read them as a two-bit number.
examples.answer: The pair Cout,S represents binary 10, correctly summing decimal 2.
examples.verification: Direct arithmetic gives 1+1+0=2; binary Cout,S=10 has the same value.

steps: Select S=A.
If A=0, output should equal B, so I₀=B.
If A=1, output should equal ¬B, so I₁=¬B. The mux equation \(\overline AI_0+AI_1\) yields XOR.

pitfalls: Output bit width must allow carry if the specification requires it.
Check active-low enables before using a decoder table.

checks.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a combinational circuit?
checks.hint: Separate current-input dependence from stored state.
checks.explanation: A combinational function depends on current inputs. Physical propagation delay exists, but there is no designed state memory.
options: It necessarily stores prior input values
Its output depends on current inputs under the ideal settled model
It requires a clock for every output change
It is the same as a flip-flop

checks.prompt: How many output lines does a complete 3-to-8 decoder have?
checks.hint: One output per input combination.
checks.explanation: \(2^3=8\) outputs.

traps.why: For inputs 1,1, a half-adder sum is 0, while OR would give 1. Carry separately represents the value 2.

traps.claim: Mux inputs must be constants
traps.why: Residual functions can be B, its complement, or other available signals when only some variables are selectors.

formulas.meaning: Full-adder outputs.

lessons.title: Sequential circuits, flip-flops and state machines
lessons.intuition: Sequential circuits combine current inputs with stored state. To reason correctly, distinguish what is stored now, what will be stored at the next clock event, and which outputs depend on inputs immediately.

sections.title: Storage elements
sections.body: A level-sensitive latch can change while its enable is active; an edge-triggered flip-flop samples around a clock edge. For D flip-flops Qnext=D; for T flip-flops Qnext=Q⊕T. JK devices hold for 00, reset for 01, set for 10 and toggle for 11. Setup and hold intervals constrain how stable inputs must be around the sampling edge.

sections.title: State-machine construction
sections.body: List states and draw input-labelled transitions. A Moore output depends only on state; a Mealy output depends on state and current input. Assign binary state codes, derive next-state/output truth tables, simplify logic and select storage. k flip-flops can encode at most 2ᵏ states, so n states require ceiling(\(\log_2 n\)) bits.

sections.title: Counters and timing
sections.body: A synchronous counter clocks all flip-flops together; ripple counters cascade transitions and have accumulated delays. A modulo-n counter uses n reachable states and returns to its start. Include reset behaviour and handle unused state codes so a stray state does not trap the machine. Clock period must allow launch, combinational delay and destination setup margin.

examples.prompt: Design the state capacity of a modulo-10 counter

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Need 10 distinct states. A modulo-10 counter must remember its current residue, so two different residues cannot share the same encoding.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Three bits encode only 8; four encode 16. The smallest sufficient bit count is the ceiling of log₂10. Rounding down fails to represent two required states.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Use 4 flip-flops and define transitions for the 6 unused codes, typically returning to a legal state. Capacity alone does not specify next-state logic. Unused encodings must have defined behavior if recovery is required.

examples.strategy: Use the number of distinguishable states to bound the required storage bits.
examples.answer: Use 4 flip-flops and define transitions for the 6 unused codes, typically returning to a legal state.
examples.verification: Four bits provide 16 encodings: 10 legal plus 6 unused. Three bits provide only 8 and cannot implement the required states.

examples.prompt: Track a T flip-flop starting at Q=0 for inputs 1,0,1
steps: First edge toggles Q to 1.
Second edge with T=0 retains 1.
Third edge toggles to 0; the final stored state is 0.

pitfalls: A latch and a flip-flop are not interchangeable timing models.
Unused binary encodings still need recovery behaviour.

checks.hint: Compare the Moore and Mealy output definitions.
checks.explanation: Moore outputs are functions of state. Mealy outputs can additionally depend directly on current input.
options: Current state and current input in its defining output function

checks.prompt: How many states can 5 flip-flops encode?
checks.hint: Every bit has two possibilities.
checks.explanation: 2⁵=32 states.

lessons.title: Fixed point, floating point and overflow
lessons.prerequisite: Binary notation and powers of two.
lessons.intuition: Bits do not have an inherent numeric interpretation. The same pattern may represent unsigned data, a signed integer, or a fraction depending on the agreed encoding. Arithmetic questions must specify width, sign convention and scaling before calculation.

sections.title: Integer representations
sections.body: Unsigned n-bit values span 0 to 2ⁿ−1. Two’s complement spans −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹−1; its most significant bit has weight −2ⁿ⁻¹. Negate within a fixed width by complementing all bits and adding 1. Sign extension repeats the sign bit to preserve a two’s-complement value. Carry-out concerns unsigned overflow; signed addition overflows when equal-sign operands produce an opposite-sign result.

sections.title: Fixed-point scaling
sections.body: With f fractional bits, interpret the stored integer as I/2ᶠ. An unsigned n-bit fixed-point format has step size 2⁻ᶠ and maximum (2ⁿ−1)/2ᶠ. Signed formats use a signed stored integer with the same scaling. Addition requires aligned scaling; multiplying two scaled integers doubles the fractional-bit count until rescaled.

sections.title: IEEE 754 single precision
sections.body: There are 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 stored fraction bits. Normal numbers have value (−1)ˢ(1.f)2^(E−127). E=0 reserves zero and subnormal values; E=255 reserves infinities and NaNs. The implicit leading 1 applies only to normals. Rounding means real-number associativity need not hold numerically.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Write +5 as 00000101. Start with the positive magnitude using exactly eight bits; the width determines both inversion and the signed range.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Invert: 11111010; add 1: 11111011. Invert every bit at that width and add one modulo 256. Merely setting the sign bit would create a different encoding system.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Decode with negative MSB weight: −128+64+32+16+8+2+1=−5. The sign bit carries weight −128; the remaining bits carry positive powers of two. This decodes the result independently.

examples.strategy: Use invert-and-add-one, then verify with the negative weight of the most significant bit.
examples.answer: Decode with negative MSB weight: −128+64+32+16+8+2+1=−5.
examples.verification: 11111011 has unsigned value 251; signed two’s complement subtracts 256, giving −5.

examples.prompt: Interpret a fixed-point stored value 24 with 4 fractional bits
steps: The scale is \(2^4=16\).
Actual value=\(24/16=1.5\).
A one-unit change in stored value changes the real value by 1/16, not by 1.

pitfalls: Two’s-complement range is asymmetric.
The implicit leading 1 is absent for subnormal floats.
Carry and signed overflow are different.

checks.prompt: When adding two signed integers, which condition signals two’s-complement signed overflow?
checks.hint: Carry and signed overflow are distinct.
checks.explanation: At fixed width, adding two positives cannot yield a true negative or two negatives a true positive; an opposite-sign encoded result signals overflow.
options: Equal-sign operands produce an opposite-sign result

checks.prompt: Stored integer 40 uses 3 fractional bits. What value does it represent?
checks.hint: Divide by 2³.

traps.why: 4-bit 1111+0001 has carry-out but represents −1+1=0 without signed overflow. 0111+0001 gives a negative pattern and signed overflow without carry-out.

name: Computer Organization & Architecture
description: Understand what happens beneath your code

lessons.title: Instruction sets, addressing modes and CPU time
lessons.intuition: An instruction is a compact command that tells a processor what operation to perform and where operands come from. Addressing modes separate operand-location rules from the operation itself. CPU performance follows the total work and cycles, not clock rate alone.

sections.title: Instruction structure
sections.body: An instruction can contain an opcode, register identifiers, addressing-mode bits and immediate/displacement fields. Load/store architectures generally operate on registers and use separate memory-transfer instructions; other architectures may permit memory operands directly. The program counter identifies instruction flow, and branches update it differently from ordinary sequential execution.

sections.title: Effective addresses
sections.body: Immediate addressing embeds the operand, not an address. Register addressing reads the register value. Direct addressing uses an explicit address; indirect addressing follows a pointer to the operand. Base+displacement computes EA=base+offset; indexed modes add an index, sometimes scaled by element size. PC-relative addressing uses a displacement from a specified PC reference point; conventions matter.

sections.title: Performance equation
sections.body: CPU time=instruction count×average CPI×cycle time=IC×CPI/frequency. For instruction classes, average CPI=Σfractionᵢ×CPIᵢ. A new design may use fewer instructions but more cycles each. Compare complete execution time and use speedup=old time/new time.

examples.prompt: Address an array element using base 1000, index 3 and 4-byte elements

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The byte displacement is 3×4=12. The address space is byte-addressed. An index counts elements, so multiplying by four converts it into bytes.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: \(EA=1000+12=1012\). The base addresses element zero; index three is the fourth element and lies twelve bytes beyond that base.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Using raw index 3 as a byte offset would fetch the wrong location. Pointer arithmetic must use units consistently: element indices cannot be added as unscaled byte offsets.

examples.strategy: Scale an element index by element width before adding the base address.
examples.answer: Using raw index 3 as a byte offset would fetch the wrong location.
examples.verification: Elements start at 1000, 1004, 1008 and 1012, so index 3 corresponds to 1012.

examples.prompt: Compute time for 2 million instructions, CPI 3, clock 1 GHz
steps: Total cycles=\(2\cdot10^6\cdot3=6\cdot10^6\).
Cycle time is \(1/10^9\) seconds.
CPU time=0.006 s=6 ms.

pitfalls: Bytes, words and elements are different address units.
Average CPI must weight instruction frequencies.

checks.prompt: With base 2000 and byte displacement 24, what is the effective address?
checks.hint: Add the displacement.

checks.prompt: A program needs 6 million cycles at 2 GHz. What is its time in milliseconds?
checks.hint: Divide cycles by cycles per second, then convert.

traps.why: A design with CPI 1 at 1 GHz is slower per instruction than CPI 1.5 at 2 GHz; instruction counts may also differ.

For the specified scaled base/index addressing form.

lessons.title: ALU design and hardwired/microprogrammed control
lessons.intuition: The datapath performs operations; the control unit chooses which operation happens and when. Keeping those roles separate makes it possible to trace an instruction as a sequence of register transfers instead of treating the CPU as a black box.

sections.title: ALU and status flags
sections.body: An ALU combines an adder, logic functions and selection hardware. Subtraction can reuse addition by complementing the second operand and setting carry-in: A−B=A+¬B+1. Flags may record zero, sign, carry and signed overflow. Signed comparison cannot rely on the sign of a wrapped subtraction without considering overflow.

sections.title: Register-transfer sequencing
sections.body: An instruction fetch can involve MAR←PC, memory read, IR←memory data and PC advancement. Execution then reads operands, activates the ALU, and writes a destination. Control signals choose mux inputs, register write enables, ALU function and memory actions. A single-cycle design combines actions in one long cycle; multicycle designs reuse hardware across shorter steps.

sections.title: Control implementation
sections.body: Hardwired control uses finite-state logic and decoding to generate signals, often with low latency but less flexibility. Microprogrammed control stores control words in a control memory; a sequencer chooses subsequent microinstructions using opcode and conditions. Horizontal microcode exposes more parallel control bits, while encoded vertical microcode reduces width at the cost of decoding.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Represent 5=0101 and 3=0011. Both operands fit in four-bit signed representation; retain that width throughout the bit calculation.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Invert 3 to 1100 and add carry-in 1: 0101+1100+1=10010. Bitwise inversion plus the carry-in forms −3 modulo 16. Include the extra carry in the intermediate sum before truncating.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Discard the carry beyond 4 bits; result 0010 is 2. The carry flag and signed-overflow flag are interpreted separately. An n-bit adder returns its low n result bits. Carry out does not by itself indicate signed overflow.

examples.strategy: Implement subtraction as addition of the width-limited two’s complement of the subtrahend.
examples.answer: Discard the carry beyond 4 bits; result 0010 is 2. The carry flag and signed-overflow flag are interpreted separately.
examples.verification: Low four bits 0010 represent +2, and +5−3 lies within the signed range −8…7, so signed overflow does not occur.

steps: Suppose there are 128 microinstructions, each 40 bits wide.
Storage is \(128\cdot40=5120\) bits.
Divide by 8 to obtain 640 bytes; sequencing circuitry is additional hardware.

pitfalls: Microinstructions and machine instructions are different levels.
Overflow interpretation depends on signedness.
revision: Datapath computes; control selects and sequences.

checks.prompt: A control store has 256 words of 32 bits. How many bytes does it occupy?
checks.hint: Multiply words by bits per word, then divide by 8.

checks.prompt: How many bits are needed to select one of 8 ALU operations?
checks.hint: Use log₂ of the number of choices.
checks.explanation: \(2^3=8\), so 3 selection bits.

method: List operands and destination, then identify the ALU operation, mux choices and write enables.
For subtraction use the fixed-width complement-plus-one construction and inspect flags separately.
For microcode storage multiply word count by control-word width; sequencing logic is separate from stored bits.

traps.claim: Microinstructions equal program instructions
traps.why: A machine instruction may require many internal microinstructions. They are different abstraction levels.

traps.claim: Signed comparison uses result sign alone
traps.why: Wrapped signed subtraction can overflow, so sign without overflow information can give the wrong comparison.

formulas.meaning: Fixed-width subtraction through an adder.
Control-memory capacity excluding additional hardware.

lessons.title: Memory hierarchy and cache mapping
lessons.prerequisite: Binary address splitting and CPU performance.
lessons.intuition: Caches exploit repetition and neighbourhood in memory accesses. A small fast store holds copies of slower memory blocks. Mapping decides where a block may go; replacement decides which resident block leaves when those allowed locations are full.

sections.title: Hierarchy and locality
sections.body: Temporal locality reuses recently accessed data; spatial locality accesses nearby addresses. Transfers occur in blocks, so one miss may bring several adjacent words. A larger block can improve spatial reuse but reduces the number of resident blocks at fixed capacity and increases transfer cost. Separate compulsory, capacity and conflict misses when reasoning about changes.

sections.title: Address partition
sections.body: In a byte-addressed system with 2ᵇ-byte blocks, the lowest b bits are block offset. A cache with S sets needs log₂S index bits; remaining high bits form the tag. Direct mapping has one line per set; W-way associativity has W lines per set. Sets=capacity/(block size×ways). Fully associative caches have one set and no index bits.

sections.title: Writes and performance
sections.body: Write-through updates lower memory on writes; write-back marks lines dirty and writes them on eviction. Write-allocate versus no-write-allocate controls write misses independently. Single-level AMAT=hit time+miss rate×miss penalty, where the penalty is the additional miss cost. Multilevel formulas require using local versus global miss rates consistently.

examples.prompt: Split a 32-bit address for a 16 KiB, 4-way cache with 64-byte blocks

steps.title: Convert capacity and count lines
steps.explanation: KiB is binary here. Data capacity excludes tag/valid metadata; do not subtract those bytes from C.

steps.title: Count sets
steps.explanation: Each set holds four lines. Index selects a set; associativity is not another independent address field.

steps.title: Find low-order fields
steps.explanation: Byte offset selects one of 64 bytes inside a block. Set index selects one of 64 sets.

steps.title: Allocate remaining address bits
steps.explanation: Tag is what remains after identifying a byte and a set. The tag comparison distinguishes different memory blocks mapping to that set.

examples.given: 32-bit byte addresses; 16 KiB data capacity; 4-way associativity; 64-byte blocks.
examples.goal: Find tag, index and offset bits.
examples.strategy: Determine sets from data capacity first, then take powers-of-two logarithms.
examples.answer: 20 tag bits, 6 index bits, 6 offset bits.
examples.verification: Reconstruct data capacity: 2⁶ sets ×4 ways ×2⁶ bytes=16,384 bytes; the fields sum to 32 bits.

examples.prompt: Compute AMAT for hit time 2 ns, miss rate 4%, penalty 50 ns
steps: Miss contribution is \(0.04\cdot50=2\) ns.
Add the baseline hit time 2 ns.
\(AMAT=4\) ns; do not multiply the hit time by hit rate in this penalty-based convention.

pitfalls: Cache capacity usually excludes tag/valid/dirty storage unless specified.
Use number of sets, not total lines, for index bits.

checks.prompt: Which quantity determines cache index bits?
checks.hint: A set-associative cache indexes a set, then compares tags within it.
checks.explanation: Index width is log₂(number of sets). Number of sets equals lines divided by ways; total lines works only in direct mapping.

checks.prompt: A hit takes 1 ns, miss rate 0.1, extra penalty 30 ns. What is AMAT in ns?
checks.hint: Use the penalty convention.

traps.claim: Use total lines for index bits in every cache
traps.why: A four-way cache has one quarter as many sets as lines. Indexing lines instead of sets steals two bits incorrectly from the tag.

traps.claim: Double-count hit time
traps.why: If miss penalty is additional cost, hit time is already paid for every access and is added once.

formulas.meaning: Byte-addressed cache: capacity C, block bytes B, ways W, address bits A.
Additional miss penalty convention.

lessons.title: Memory interfacing, interrupts and DMA
lessons.intuition: A processor must select the correct memory device and coordinate data transfer. I/O introduces devices whose speed and readiness differ from the CPU. Polling, interrupts and DMA assign different amounts of coordination work to software and hardware.

sections.title: Memory organization and decoding
sections.body: A memory specified as N×w stores N locations of w bits each. Address bits select locations; data pins carry width w. To expand width, connect chips to different data-bit lanes while sharing address lines. To expand depth, decode extra high address bits into chip-select signals. Byte addressing may require multiple byte lanes and enables.

sections.title: Polling and interrupts
sections.body: Polling repeatedly checks a device status register and spends CPU cycles waiting. An interrupt lets a device request attention; the CPU saves required execution state, enters an interrupt handler, services the event and returns. Masking, priority and nesting determine which interrupts can be serviced. Interrupt latency includes finishing or suspending permitted work and reaching the handler.

sections.title: DMA
sections.body: A DMA controller transfers blocks between a device and memory after the CPU configures addresses, length and direction. Burst mode may occupy a bus for a sequence; cycle stealing interleaves transfers with CPU activity. DMA reduces per-byte CPU overhead but does not imply zero setup cost or unlimited bandwidth. Shared caches can require coherency handling for DMA buffers.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Width expansion requires 16/8=2 chips in parallel per bank. Two chips receive the same address and supply different byte lanes to build each 16-bit word.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Depth expansion requires 4K/1K=4 banks. Four independent banks provide four times the word count. Bank selection must enable only the addressed bank.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Total=2×4=8 chips; two extra address bits select the bank, while ten bits select a location inside a chip. Multiplying the two expansion factors counts all physical chips; address bits select words, not individual bit lanes.

examples.strategy: Separate word-width expansion from the number of addressable words.
examples.answer: Total=2×4=8 chips; two extra address bits select the bank, while ten bits select a location inside a chip.
examples.verification: Eight chips each store 1024×8 bits, totaling 65536 bits; the target 4096×16 bits has the same capacity.

examples.prompt: Compare one-byte interrupts with DMA for 4096 bytes
steps: An interrupt per byte produces 4096 service events.
A DMA block can use one setup and a completion interrupt under the simple model.
The CPU saves many handler invocations, although memory-bus transfer time remains.

pitfalls: Chip width and depth expansion are separate factors.
DMA still competes for memory bandwidth.
revision: Total chips=(desired depth/chip depth)×(desired width/chip width).
Interrupts request service; DMA performs data movement.

checks.prompt: What is the primary role of DMA?
checks.hint: The CPU configures transfer work but need not move each byte.
checks.explanation: DMA transfers between devices and memory with controller support. Setup/completion overhead and bus competition still remain.
options: Transfer blocks with reduced per-byte CPU involvement

checks.prompt: How many address bits select one location in a 4K-location chip?
checks.explanation: 4096=2¹², requiring 12 address bits.

traps.claim: DMA means the CPU pays no cost
traps.why: The CPU configures transfers and handles completion, and DMA can compete for memory bandwidth.

traps.claim: Chip count depends only on bytes
traps.why: Two organizations with the same byte capacity may need different bank/wiring arrangements when depth and width are specified.

formulas.meaning: For integral compatible depth/width expansion.
Address bits for D locations, when D is a power of two.

lessons.title: Instruction pipelining and hazards
lessons.intuition: Pipelining overlaps different instructions in different stages. It increases completed instructions per unit time, while each individual instruction still passes through every stage. Hazards arise when that ideal overlap would violate resource limits or program dependencies.

sections.title: Ideal timing
sections.body: For k equal-latency stages and n instructions, an initially empty ideal pipeline takes k+n−1 cycles. The first instruction fills the pipeline; each subsequent one then finishes one cycle later. Clock period is determined by the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead, not average stage delay. Unequal stages reduce ideal speedup.

sections.title: Data and structural hazards
sections.body: A structural hazard occurs when simultaneous operations need the same unavailable resource. A RAW dependency requires a consumer to receive the producer’s value; forwarding can route it before register writeback. A load-use pair can still stall if data arrives after the consumer needs it. WAR and WAW are naming/order hazards relevant to designs that reorder reads or writes; simple in-order pipelines handle them differently.

sections.title: Control hazards
sections.body: A branch may make fetched instructions wrong-path work. Waiting, predicting, or delayed-branch mechanisms handle this in different models. A misprediction flushes invalid instructions and adds cycles. To compute effective CPI, add expected stall cycles per instruction from hazards without double-counting overlapping penalties.

examples.prompt: A 5-stage pipeline runs 12 instructions with 3 total stall cycles

steps.title: Count the ideal cycles
steps.explanation: The first instruction needs five cycles. Each remaining instruction adds one cycle in this single-issue, balanced-stage model.

steps.title: Include stalls
steps.explanation: The question supplies total actual stalls, so add them once. They are not three stalls per instruction.

steps.title: Convert cycles to time
steps.explanation: Pipeline overlap changes instruction throughput; multiplying every instruction by all five stage times would erase that overlap.

examples.given: Five stages; 12 instructions; three actual stall cycles; cycle time 2 ns.
examples.goal: Find elapsed time including fill and drain.
examples.strategy: Count pipeline cycles before multiplying by the cycle duration.
examples.answer: 19 cycles, 38 ns.
examples.verification: With one instruction and no stalls the same formula gives five cycles, matching its complete path through the stages.

examples.prompt: A branch frequency is 20%, misprediction rate 10%, penalty 3 cycles
steps: Mispredictions per instruction=\(0.2\cdot0.1=0.02\).
Expected additional CPI=\(0.02\cdot3=0.06\).
If baseline CPI is 1 and there are no other stalls, effective CPI=1.06.

pitfalls: Dependency does not automatically mean a stall if forwarding meets timing.
Pipeline speedup is not simply stage count for short sequences.
revision: Clock period follows the slowest stage.

checks.prompt: Does a RAW dependency necessarily cause a stall?
checks.hint: Distinguish logical dependency from timing availability.
checks.explanation: Forwarding can resolve many RAW dependencies without a stall. A load-use timing gap may still require one in the specified pipeline.
options: No; forwarding may deliver the value on time

checks.prompt: A sequence ideally needs 20 cycles and adds 4 nonoverlapping stalls. What is its total?
checks.hint: Add actual stalls once.
checks.explanation: 20+4=24 cycles.

name: Programming & Data Structures
description: Build a strong foundation in C and structures

lessons.title: C types, expressions, pointers and memory
lessons.intuition: C exposes the relationship between a value and its storage. A pointer stores an address; dereferencing accesses the object there. Tracing code requires tracking types, lifetimes and sequencing, rather than assuming every expression has a predictable machine result.

sections.title: Types and evaluation
sections.body: Integer promotions and conversions affect arithmetic. Integer division truncates toward zero; floating operands change division behaviour. Logical AND and logical OR short-circuit, evaluating the right side only when necessary. sizeof measures bytes and normally does not evaluate its operand, except relevant variable-length-array cases. Do not assume int is always four bytes unless the question states the machine model.

sections.title: Pointers and arrays
sections.body: For a pointer p to T, p+1 advances by sizeof(T) bytes within a valid array range. An array expression usually decays to a pointer to its first element, but sizeof on an actual in-scope array returns full array size. Function parameters written as arrays are adjusted to pointers. Dereferencing a one-past-the-end pointer is invalid even though forming it is permitted.

sections.title: Lifetime and undefined behaviour
sections.body: Automatic local objects cease to exist after their scope exits; returning their addresses creates dangling pointers. Dynamically allocated storage survives until freed and must be checked for allocation failure. Out-of-bounds accesses and unsequenced conflicting modifications can be undefined behaviour. For such programs, reporting a single numerical output is not a valid analysis.

sections.title: A safe pointer trace
sections.body: Use a table of variable, type, value and referenced object. In the example, a is an array object, p points to its second element, and *p refers to a[1]. After *p=9, the array changes without changing p. Moving p by one advances to a[2]; it does not increase the integer stored at a[1]. A pointer may be formed one past the array, but that location is not an element to dereference. The code deliberately separates updates into sequenced statements to avoid unsequenced modification traps.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: For int a[5], sizeof(a)=5×4=20 bytes while a remains an array in scope. sizeof sees an actual array object in this scope and counts all five elements, with no array-to-pointer conversion.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: If p=&a[1], p+2 points to a[3], advancing 8 bytes. Adding two to an int pointer advances by two int objects, not two bytes. The resulting pointer remains inside the array.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Inside a function f(int a[]), sizeof(a) is pointer size, not 20. An array-form parameter declaration is adjusted to a pointer parameter. Its sizeof therefore uses the platform’s pointer width.

examples.strategy: Track array extent, pointer scaling and parameter adjustment as separate C rules.
examples.answer: Inside a function f(int a[]), sizeof(a) is pointer size, not 20.
examples.verification: From &a[1], two further element positions lead to &a[3]; byte displacement is 2×4=8.

steps: 7 and 2 are integer operands, so 7/2 gives 3.
2.0 is floating; 7 is converted and division gives 3.5.
Assigning the first expression to double afterward produces 3.0; conversion does not restore the discarded fraction.

pitfalls: Address arithmetic scales by pointed-to type size.
Do not compute outputs for undefined behaviour.
Assignment target type does not retroactively change integer division.
revision: sizeof(array)=element count×element size in array scope.
C arguments are passed by value; a copied pointer can still mutate its pointee.

checks.hint: Array parameter syntax is adjusted.
checks.explanation: The parameter is adjusted to int*. sizeof(a) there measures pointer size, not the original caller array storage.

checks.prompt: In C, what is the value of 9/4 when both operands are int?
checks.hint: Integer division truncates toward zero.
checks.explanation: 9/4 is 2, with remainder 1.

lessons.title: Recursion and stack-frame tracing
lessons.intuition: A recursive call is another invocation with its own local state. You can reason inductively about the returned value or mechanically trace stack frames. Both require knowing where recursion stops and how an argument gets closer to that base case.

sections.title: Call and return model
sections.body: Each call creates a frame with parameters, locals and return information. A recursive call suspends its caller until it returns. For factorial, fact(n) waits for fact(n−1), then multiplies. Statements before recursion run on descent; statements after recursion run during unwinding. Shared global state differs from per-frame locals.

sections.title: Correctness and termination
sections.body: State a base case and a decreasing measure bounded below, such as remaining input length. An induction proof assumes smaller calls work and verifies the current combination. Recursion over graph edges needs a visited set when cycles are possible; merely calling neighbours is not guaranteed to terminate.

sections.title: Time versus space
sections.body: Count the total calls for time and maximum simultaneous active frames for stack space. Factorial takes \(\Theta(n)\) time and \(\Theta(n)\) stack. A balanced divide recursion can take \(\Theta(n)\) total work but \(\Theta(\log n)\) stack depth. Naive Fibonacci revisits subproblems exponentially; memoization stores repeated results and reduces time to \(\Theta(n)\).

sections.title: A recursion template you can trace
sections.body: The base case returns before making another call. For n>0, n−1 is a smaller nonnegative input, so the decreasing argument guarantees reaching zero. The multiplication waits for the child call to return. This mathematical template assumes the answer fits in the return type: a real C implementation can overflow for sufficiently large n, and the allowed range must be part of its contract.

examples.prompt: Trace f(n): if n=0 return; print n; f(n−1); print n, starting at 2

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Call f(2) prints 2, then calls f(1), which prints 1. The first print occurs before recursion, so descending calls produce decreasing values.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: f(0) immediately returns; f(1) then prints 1. The base case prints nothing. Returning resumes f(1) after its call statement, rather than restarting the function.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: f(2) resumes and prints 2, giving 2,1,1,2. The final print belongs to the suspended outer frame; it runs only after the inner call has completed.

examples.strategy: Maintain one program position per active call and resume after the recursive call returns.
examples.answer: f(2) resumes and prints 2, giving 2,1,1,2.
examples.verification: Each nonbase call prints twice. Two such calls give four values, and the before/after arrangement makes 2,1,1,2 symmetric.

examples.prompt: Count calls in factorial(4) with base factorial(0)
steps: The active call chain is 4→3→2→1→0.
There are 5 calls and maximum stack depth 5 under this model.
Unwinding returns 1,1,2,6,24. Do not count only the 4 multiplications as the number of calls.

pitfalls: Count base-case invocations too.
Total call count and stack depth need not have the same asymptotic size.
revision: Recursion needs a base case and progress.
Time counts work; stack space counts the deepest active chain.

checks.prompt: Which determines auxiliary recursive stack use?
checks.hint: Frames are released when calls finish.
checks.explanation: Stack space follows simultaneously active frames. Many sequential recursive calls may reuse storage, so total calls alone does not give stack size.
options: Maximum simultaneous call depth and per-frame storage

checks.prompt: A recurrence T(n)=T(n−1)+1 has T(0)=1. What is T(8)?
checks.hint: One unit is added for each level.

For factorial, fact(n) waits for fact(n−1), then multiplies. Statements before recursion run on descent; statements after recursion run during unwinding. Shared global state differs from per-frame locals. State a base case and a decreasing measure bounded below, such as remaining input length. An induction proof assumes smaller calls work and verifies the current combination. Recursion over graph edges needs a visited set when cycles are possible; merely calling neighbours is not guaranteed to terminate. Count the total calls for time and maximum simultaneous active frames for stack space. Factorial takes \(\Theta(n)\) time and \(\Theta(n)\) stack. A balanced divide recursion can take \(\Theta(n)\) total work but \(\Theta(\log n)\) stack depth. Naive Fibonacci revisits subproblems exponentially; memoization stores repeated results and reduces time to \(\Theta(n)\). The base case returns before making another call. For n>0, n−1 is a smaller nonnegative input, so the decreasing argument guarantees reaching zero. The multiplication waits for the child call to return. This mathematical template assumes the answer fits in the return type: a real C implementation can overflow for sufficiently large n, and the allowed range must be part of its contract.
lessons.example: Trace f(n): if n=0 return; print n; f(n−1); print n, starting at 2

gateGuide.recognize: Separate descent from return-time work. Trace invocations, not just function names, because each call has its own frame.
method: Write the base case and decreasing measure, then draw the active call chain or tree.
Execute statements before recursion on descent and after recursion while unwinding.
Count total call/work nodes for time, but only the maximum simultaneous active chain for stack space.

traps.claim: Call count equals stack depth
traps.why: A branching recursion may make many sequential calls while retaining only one root-to-leaf chain at a time.

traps.claim: A recursive formula guarantees termination
traps.why: If arguments do not decrease to a valid base case, it may loop or exhaust stack rather than compute the intended sequence.

lessons.title: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues
lessons.intuition: Data structures trade access speed against update cost. A complexity statement must specify what information you already possess: inserting after a known linked-list node is cheap, but finding that node may dominate the operation.

sections.title: Arrays and linked lists
sections.body: Contiguous arrays allow constant-time indexed access because address=base+index×element size. Middle insertion shifts a suffix, taking \(\Theta(n)\). A singly linked list stores a next pointer and supports \(O(1)\) insertion after a known node. Finding a predecessor or an indexed element takes \(O(n)\). Doubly linked lists store previous links too, enabling deletion of a known node without a predecessor search.

sections.title: Stacks and queues
sections.body: Stacks remove the most recently inserted item and support recursion, expression evaluation and DFS. Queues remove the oldest and support BFS. A linked queue can enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head in \(O(1)\) with both pointers. Reversing these ends in a singly linked list makes tail deletion expensive.

sections.title: Circular arrays
sections.body: Advance queue indices modulo capacity. Empty and full can both appear as head=tail unless you track a count, a full flag, or leave one slot unused. A capacity-n array with an unused-slot convention holds only n−1 elements. Carefully check whether an index denotes the next free location or the last occupied location.

sections.title: Linked queue operation sequence
sections.body: To enqueue a node, initialize its next pointer to NULL, attach it after the current tail if one exists, or make it the head for an empty queue; then update tail. To dequeue, read the head node, advance head to its next, and if the queue becomes empty set tail to NULL as well. Save the returned value before freeing the removed node. These pointer operations are \(O(1)\) because no predecessor search is required. A nonempty invariant is that tail points to the final node and tail.next is NULL. The empty invariant has both pointers NULL. Missing the final tail reset leaves a dangling pointer after removing the last node.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Push 2 then 3; + pops both and pushes 5. Operands are pushed in encounter order. Addition removes two values and replaces them with one, reducing stack size by one.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Push 4; * pops 4 and 5 and pushes 20. The earlier addition’s result is an operand for multiplication, so postfix order directly represents evaluation dependencies.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The final stack contains 20. For subtraction preserve left/right operand order when popping. A well-formed binary postfix expression finishes with exactly one value. The first popped operand is the right operand.

examples.strategy: Trace a stack after every token; operators consume operands and push their result.
examples.answer: The final stack contains 20. For subtraction preserve left/right operand order when popping.
examples.verification: The equivalent infix expression is (2+3)×4=20. For “2 3 −”, correct popping gives 2−3=−1, not 1.

examples.prompt: A queue has capacity 5 and next-free tail index 4. Enqueue twice
steps: The first insertion uses slot 4 and advances tail to (4+1)%5=0.
The second uses slot 0 and advances tail to 1.
The wrap is arithmetic modulo capacity; valid insertion also requires checking available space.

pitfalls: List insertion is not \(O(1)\) if the position first needs a search.
Circular queue capacity depends on the chosen full/empty convention.

checks.prompt: To implement a singly linked queue efficiently with head/tail pointers, which ends are used?
checks.hint: Tail deletion needs finding its predecessor in a singly linked list.
checks.explanation: Tail insertion and head deletion take \(O(1)\) with maintained pointers. The reverse requires predecessor traversal for dequeue.
options: Search the entire list for every enqueue

checks.hint: Use modulo 8.

traps.why: Finding the kth node first takes O(n); only insertion after an already-known node is constant time.

lessons.title: Trees, traversals and binary search trees
lessons.intuition: A tree is a connected acyclic structure. Rooting it introduces parents, children and subtrees. Binary search trees add an ordering invariant, so searching can discard one entire subtree at each comparison—but only balanced height guarantees logarithmic depth.

sections.title: Tree terminology and traversals
sections.body: Height in edges is the longest root-to-leaf edge count; some problems instead count nodes, so read the convention. Preorder visits root,left,right; inorder left,root,right; postorder left,right,root. A binary tree has at most two children per node. A full binary tree gives each internal node exactly two children; a complete tree fills levels left to right.

sections.title: BST operations
sections.body: For distinct keys, everything in a node’s left subtree is smaller and everything in the right is larger. Search follows one comparison-directed path. Insertion finds a null child location. Deletion handles no child, one child, or two children; the two-child case replaces the key with inorder successor or predecessor and deletes that replacement node.

sections.title: Complexity and reconstruction
sections.body: Search, insertion and deletion take O(h). Sorted insertion into an unbalanced BST can create h=n−1. Balanced trees maintain logarithmic height. Inorder traversal produces sorted keys, not insertion order. With distinct keys, inorder plus preorder or postorder uniquely determine a binary tree; preorder alone generally does not determine an arbitrary binary tree.

sections.title: Why traversal order changes output
sections.body: The recursive structure is the same for all three depth-first traversals; only the placement of visit(root) changes. Put it before the two recursive calls for preorder, between them for inorder, or afterward for postorder. On a BST, the between placement visits every smaller left key, then the root, then every larger right key, proving sorted output by induction. All three traversals visit each node once and take \(\Theta(n)\) time; auxiliary recursive space is Θ(h), which is \(\Theta(n)\) for a chain and \(\Theta(\log n)\) for a balanced tree.
sections.code:
inorder(node):
    if node is null: return
    inorder(node.left)
    visit(node.key)
    inorder(node.right)

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: 4 becomes root; 2 goes left; 6 goes right. Each new key follows smaller-left and larger-right from the root, so insertion order determines shape.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: 1 goes left of 2 and 3 right of 2. Once at node 2, keys 1 and 3 are compared with 2; both still belong in the left subtree of 4.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Inorder is 1,2,3,4,6; preorder is 4,2,1,3,6. Trace the visit rule rather than memorizing a shape. Inorder visits left/node/right; preorder visits node/left/right. Applying those rules yields different sequences.

examples.strategy: Insert by comparisons, then use traversal visit rules rather than the order of insertion.
examples.answer: Inorder is 1,2,3,4,6; preorder is 4,2,1,3,6. Trace the visit rule rather than memorizing a shape.
examples.verification: The inorder sequence is sorted, which checks the BST invariant. The preorder starts with root 4, as required by its visit rule.

examples.prompt: Delete root 4 from that tree using its successor
steps: The smallest key in the right subtree is 6.
Replace 4 by 6 and delete the old leaf containing 6.
The remaining root 6 has the original left subtree and no right child; the BST invariant remains true.

pitfalls: Complete, full and perfect trees are different definitions.
A BST is not automatically balanced.
revision: Perfect binary tree nodes=2^(h+1)−1 for edge-height h.

checks.explanation: Inorder visits left, root, right, yielding keys in increasing order under the BST invariant.

checks.hint: Ascending keys create a right chain.
checks.explanation: Four nodes on one path contain 3 edges.
