traps.why: Ascending insertions can create a chain and linear-height search.

traps.claim: Complete means full
traps.why: A complete tree fills levels left to right; a full tree requires every internal node have two children. Neither definition can substitute for the other.

formulas.meaning: Edge-height h convention for a perfect binary tree.
Search/insertion/deletion costs before assuming balance.

lessons.title: Binary heaps and graph representations
lessons.intuition: A heap guarantees an extreme value at the root without sorting the entire collection. Graph representations instead organize many-to-many links. In both cases, choosing a representation determines which operations are cheap and which information must be searched.

sections.title: Heap invariants
sections.body: A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree whose parent key is no larger than its child keys. In a zero-based array, left child=2i+1, right child=2i+2 and parent=floor((i−1)/2). Completeness gives height \(\Theta(\log n)\). Sibling order is unrestricted and a heap is not a BST.

sections.title: Heap updates and construction
sections.body: Insertion appends and bubbles upward; delete-min swaps the final element to the root and sifts downward. Each traverses at most the height. Bottom-up construction sifts internal nodes from the last parent backward. It is \(\Theta(n)\), since many nodes have tiny subtrees; multiplying n by the maximum sift cost overestimates aggregate work.

sections.title: Graph storage
sections.body: An adjacency matrix uses Θ(V²) space and permits \(O(1)\) edge tests, but listing neighbours takes Θ(V). Adjacency lists use Θ(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours proportional to degree. An undirected graph usually stores each edge twice in lists. Weighted graphs attach weights; directed graphs distinguish outgoing from incoming edges.

sections.title: Why build-heap is linear
sections.body: Only about n/2 nodes have height zero, at most n/4 have height one, at most n/8 have height two, and so on. A sift from height h costs O(h), so aggregate work is bounded by n times Σh/2^(h+1), a convergent constant sum. Thus bottom-up build is \(O(n)\), unlike repeatedly inserting n elements, whose simple worst-case bound is \(O(n\log n)\). The algorithm starts at the last internal node, floor(n/2)−1 in zero-based indexing, and visits parents backward. Each node’s child subtrees are already heaps before it is sifted, which is the key invariant.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Append to get [3,5,4,2]. Appending in array order fills the next complete-tree position; inserting arbitrarily would break the shape property.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Parent of index 3 is 1; swap 2 with 5 to obtain [3,2,4,5]. For zero-based indexing the parent is floor((i−1)/2). Compare with that parent and swap only when heap order is violated.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Parent of index 1 is 0; swap 2 with 3 to obtain [2,3,4,5]. Heap order is restored. The second swap reaches the root. Other branches were already ordered and do not need global sorting.

examples.strategy: Append to preserve completeness, then repair heap order only along the ancestor path.
examples.answer: Parent of index 1 is 0; swap 2 with 3 to obtain [2,3,4,5]. Heap order is restored.
examples.verification: In [2,3,4,5], 2≤3, 2≤4 and 3≤5, so all parent-child inequalities hold; a heap need not be a fully sorted array.

steps: A full adjacency matrix allocates 1000000 cells.
Adjacency-list edge entries are 2000 directed or 4000 undirected, plus vertex headers.
Sparse connectivity strongly favours list space, though a matrix provides constant-time edge membership tests.

pitfalls: Heap order does not sort siblings or support BST-style search.
Array child formulas change for one-based indexing.
revision: List space Θ(V+E), matrix space Θ(V²).

checks.prompt: Which complexity describes bottom-up binary heap construction?
checks.hint: Sum work over node heights rather than maximum height times all nodes.
checks.explanation: Most nodes have small height; the weighted height sum is linear. Repeated insertion is a different construction method.

checks.prompt: An undirected graph has 7 edges. How many neighbour entries are stored in ordinary adjacency lists?
checks.hint: Store each edge at both endpoints.
checks.explanation: 2×7=14 entries.

name: Algorithms
description: Learn to choose, prove and analyze algorithms

lessons.title: Asymptotic time, space and recurrences
lessons.intuition: Asymptotic analysis studies how cost grows with input size. It abstracts constants but must still describe the operation being measured and the case: worst-case, average-case or amortized. A bound without those assumptions can mislead.

sections.title: Bounds and cases
sections.body: f=O(g) means f is eventually at most a constant multiple of g; Ω is a lower bound and Θ is both. A worst-case time function maximizes over size-n inputs. Average-case needs an input distribution; amortized cost averages over an operation sequence without necessarily involving randomness. Best-case \(O(n)\) does not imply worst-case \(O(n)\).

sections.title: Loops and recursion
sections.body: Consecutive loops add costs; nested loops sum inner counts. A triangular loop executes Σᵢ₌₁ⁿi=\(\frac{n(n+1)}2\) operations. Halving a variable repeatedly yields \(\Theta(\log n)\) iterations. For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), compare f with n^(log_b a) under the Master theorem’s applicable conditions; irregular recurrences may need a recursion tree or substitution.

sections.title: Space accounting
sections.body: Report input storage and auxiliary storage separately. Recursive stack memory follows the maximum active depth and frame size. Sequential calls reuse stack space once previous calls return. An algorithm can run \(\Theta(n\log n)\) total time with only \(\Theta(\log n)\) recursive stack if frames use constant additional space and divide inputs without copying.

sections.title: A recursion-tree comparison
sections.body: T(n)=T(n/2)+1 does constant work at each of \(\log_2 n\) levels, giving \(\Theta(\log n)\). T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 has increasingly many nodes and \(\Theta(n)\) total calls. \(T(n)=2T(n/2)+n\) has total n work at each of logarithmically many levels, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\). All three have logarithmic depth, demonstrating why depth is not a time bound. For an iterative doubling loop i=1;i<n;i*=2, iterations also grow logarithmically; a triangular incrementing loop instead requires summing linearly increasing counts. Specify input size in units that match the algorithm: numeric value n and bit length log n are not the same complexity parameter.

examples.prompt: Analyse for i=1..n, for j=1..i, one operation

steps.title: Express the work as a sum
steps.explanation: The inner loop length depends on i, so n×n is an upper bound but not the exact count.

steps.title: Evaluate the arithmetic series
steps.explanation: Pairing first and last terms gives average (n+1)/2 across n terms.

steps.title: Establish a tight bound
steps.explanation: Both upper and lower bounds are quadratic. Θ, rather than only O, expresses this tight order.

examples.given: For each i=1,…,n, the inner loop performs i constant-time operations.
examples.goal: Find the total operation count and tight asymptotic growth.
examples.strategy: Sum the changing inner bound; nesting alone does not specify the exact count.

examples.verification: For n=3, counts 1+2+3=6 agree with 3×4/2. Loop-control overhead has the same asymptotic order.

steps: Each recursion level performs total n combining work.
There are \(\log_2 n\) levels before constant-size leaves.
Total is \(\Theta(n\log n)\); a balanced recursion uses \(\Theta(\log n)\) stack depth with constant-size frames.

pitfalls: Do not confuse maximum depth with total call count.
Big-O alone does not assert a tight bound.
revision: Time counts all work; auxiliary space counts simultaneous storage.

traps.why: An inner loop may halve, depend on i, or have a constant range; count its actual operations.

traps.claim: Numeric n and bit length n are interchangeable

lessons.title: Searching and sorting with invariants
lessons.intuition: A search or sort is easier to understand through its invariant: what remains true after every iteration or recursive step. Complexity then follows from how fast the unresolved region shrinks and how much work is done to combine results.

sections.title: Binary search
sections.body: Maintain a range that could contain the key in sorted data. Compare its midpoint, discard the half ruled out by ordering, and update bounds so the loop progresses. After k comparisons the candidate range is about n/2ᵏ, producing \(\Theta(\log n)\) worst-case time. Unsorted input destroys the discard argument. Boundary variants such as first occurrence need their own invariant.

sections.title: Comparison sorts
sections.body: Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each new key, giving \(\Theta(n^2)\) worst-case and \(\Theta(n)\) best-case on already sorted input. Merge sort recursively sorts halves and linearly merges them, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) and ordinarily \(\Theta(n)\) auxiliary array storage. Heapsort builds a heap then repeatedly extracts, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) worst-case and an in-place array implementation.

sections.title: Quicksort and lower bounds
sections.body: Partition around a pivot, then recurse on both sides. Balanced partitions produce \(\Theta(n\log n)\); consistently extreme pivots produce \(\Theta(n^2)\). Randomization gives expected \(\Theta(n\log n)\), not a worst-case guarantee. General comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case; counting/radix sorts exploit additional assumptions and are not counterexamples.

sections.title: Binary search with terminating bounds
sections.body: This version keeps an inclusive range [lo,hi]. On a failed comparison it removes the midpoint as well as the impossible half, ensuring progress even when one or two candidates remain. The midpoint formula avoids unnecessarily adding two large indices in fixed-width arithmetic. The returned −1 distinguishes absence from valid zero-based index 0. Sorting the input is a prerequisite; this routine does not verify that condition.
sections.code:
binary_search(a, key):
    lo = 0; hi = length(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + floor((hi-lo)/2)
        if a[mid] == key: return mid
        if a[mid] < key: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

lessons.concept: A search or sort is easier to understand through its invariant: what remains true after every iteration or recursive step. Complexity then follows from how fast the unresolved region shrinks and how much work is done to combine results.
lessons.method: Maintain a range that could contain the key in sorted data. Compare its midpoint, discard the half ruled out by ordering, and update bounds so the loop progresses. After k comparisons the candidate range is about n/2ᵏ, producing \(\Theta(\log n)\) worst-case time. Unsorted input destroys the discard argument. Boundary variants such as first occurrence need their own invariant. Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each new key, giving \(\Theta(n^2)\) worst-case and \(\Theta(n)\) best-case on already sorted input. Merge sort recursively sorts halves and linearly merges them, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) and ordinarily \(\Theta(n)\) auxiliary array storage. Heapsort builds a heap then repeatedly extracts, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) worst-case and an in-place array implementation. Partition around a pivot, then recurse on both sides. Balanced partitions produce \(\Theta(n\log n)\); consistently extreme pivots produce \(\Theta(n^2)\). Randomization gives expected \(\Theta(n\log n)\), not a worst-case guarantee. General comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case; counting/radix sorts exploit additional assumptions and are not counterexamples. This version keeps an inclusive range [lo,hi]. On a failed comparison it removes the midpoint as well as the impossible half, ensuring progress even when one or two candidates remain. The midpoint formula avoids unnecessarily adding two large indices in fixed-width arithmetic. The returned −1 distinguishes absence from valid zero-based index 0. Sorting the input is a prerequisite; this routine does not verify that condition.

lessons.title: Hashing, collisions and probing
lessons.intuition: A hash function chooses a bucket from a key. Different keys may choose the same bucket, so collision resolution is part of the data structure, not an exceptional error. Expected constant-time behaviour depends on hashing quality and load, not just using the word “hash”.

sections.title: Separate chaining
sections.body: Each bucket holds a collection of colliding entries. With m buckets and n keys, load factor α=n/m is the average chain length. Under a uniform hashing assumption, searches take expected O(1+α). Chaining permits α>1, while long or adversarially concentrated chains can still produce \(O(n)\) worst-case search.

sections.title: Open addressing
sections.body: All entries occupy slots in the array. Linear probing tries h(k),h(k)+1,… modulo m, causing primary clustering. Quadratic probing and double hashing use different probe sequences with coverage conditions. The table must have empty space for ordinary insertion; load factor approaches 1 with worsening probe costs.

sections.title: Deletion and invariants
sections.body: An unsuccessful search can stop at a never-used empty slot. Deleting by making a slot simply empty can break a probe chain and hide later entries. Use a tombstone or a correct relocation strategy. Resizing rehashes existing keys because the mapping depends on the new capacity; copying old slot positions is not sufficient.

sections.title: A probing trace with wraparound
sections.body: With capacity 7 and h(k)=k mod 7, insert 6,13,20,27 by linear probing. All initially choose slot 6. The first occupies 6; the second wraps to 0; the third checks 6,0 and occupies 1; the fourth occupies 2. This creates a cluster spanning the boundary. Searching for absent key 34 probes those occupied slots before reaching empty slot 3. The cost depends on occupied runs, not simply whether its initial hash is in range. A tombstone should not stop unsuccessful search, but insertion may remember its position for reuse while continuing sufficiently far to rule out an existing duplicate key.

steps.title: Apply the rule

steps.title: Interpret the result

lessons.title: Greedy and divide-and-conquer design
lessons.intuition: Divide-and-conquer solves smaller problems and combines their answers. Greedy algorithms instead commit to a local choice without revisiting it. A plausible local rule is not enough: prove why an optimal solution can include that choice.

sections.title: Divide-and-conquer pattern
sections.body: Define a base case, split into smaller subproblems, recursively solve, and combine. Merge sort uses two independent halves; binary search recurses into only one. Write a recurrence including the combine cost. Balanced splitting gives shallow recursion; an unbalanced split may erase the expected benefit.

sections.title: Greedy correctness
sections.body: State the local choice and residual problem. An exchange argument takes an optimal solution and replaces part of it with the greedy choice without worsening its objective, then applies induction. In activity selection, choosing the earliest-finishing compatible activity leaves the largest opportunity for subsequent activities.

sections.title: Where greedy fails
sections.body: Fractional knapsack sorts by value/weight ratio because fractional exchange is allowed. 0/1 knapsack forbids splitting, so the same strategy can miss a better combination. A counterexample is sufficient to disprove an unsupported greedy rule. MST algorithms work because cut/cycle properties justify their choices, not because every weighted optimization is greedy-solvable.

steps.title: Order by finish time
steps.explanation: Finishing earlier leaves at least as much room for later activities. An optimal solution’s first activity can be replaced by this earliest finisher without reducing how many later activities fit.

steps.title: Select and update the boundary
steps.explanation: Compatibility is start≥last selected finish. After taking [3,4], the interval [2,5] starts too early and overlaps.

steps.title: Complete the selection
steps.explanation: Equal endpoints are allowed by the stated convention. Under strict non-touching semantics these choices would need a different feasibility test.

examples.verification: All four cannot be selected because [2,5] overlaps [1,3] and [3,4]. A feasible size-three solution attains the largest remaining possible count.

lessons.title: Dynamic programming from state to solution
lessons.intuition: Dynamic programming remembers answers to overlapping subproblems. Its difficult part is choosing what information a state must retain. Begin with a precise meaning for each table entry; a recurrence is valid only if it considers every allowed final choice.

sections.title: State and transition
sections.body: Define state variables, then express an answer using smaller states. For 0/1 knapsack dp[i,w] is maximum value using the first i items within capacity w. Skipping item i gives dp[i−1,w]; including it, when feasible, gives valueᵢ+dp[i−1,w−weightᵢ]. The maximum covers both possibilities.

sections.title: Base cases and ordering
sections.body: For knapsack, dp[0,w]=0 and dp[i,0]=0 when item weights are positive. Bottom-up order must make dependencies available; memoized recursion computes states on demand. A one-dimensional 0/1 knapsack update processes capacities downward so an item is not used multiple times in the same iteration. Upward updates correspond to a different reuse model.

sections.title: Cost and reconstruction
sections.body: Complexity is number of reachable states times transition cost, not simply recursion depth. O(nW) knapsack depends on numeric capacity W and is pseudopolynomial in its binary encoding length. To recover selected items, record choices or compare table entries and walk backwards. Finding only the optimal value need not reveal a unique solution.

sections.title: 0/1 knapsack in one dimension
sections.body: Process capacities downward so dp[w−weight] still refers to the state before the current item was introduced. An upward loop could read a value updated earlier during the same item and count that item again. For a single item weight 2,value 3 and capacity 4, downward iteration gives dp[4]=3 and dp[2]=3; upward iteration can incorrectly produce dp[4]=6 for a 0/1 problem.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: After the first item, capacities 2,3,4 can achieve value 3. Each state summarizes an optimum under a specific prefix/capacity restriction; this meaning prevents accidental item reuse.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: For the second item at capacity 4, skipping gives 3; including gives 4+dp[1,1]=4. The include branch uses remaining capacity and the preceding item prefix, while the exclude branch keeps capacity unchanged.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Optimal value is 4. Both items do not fit because their total weight is 5. Taking the better feasible branch explores both possibilities for the last item rather than committing to a local ratio choice.

examples.answer: Optimal value is 4. Both items do not fit because their total weight is 5.

lessons.title: Graph traversal, MSTs and shortest paths
lessons.prerequisite: Graph representations, heaps and greedy proofs.
lessons.intuition: Graph traversal answers reachability; shortest paths minimize route cost; a minimum spanning tree minimizes the total cost of connecting every vertex. These objectives differ, so an MST path need not be a shortest path.

sections.title: BFS and DFS
sections.body: BFS uses a queue and discovers vertices in layers, giving shortest edge-count paths in an unweighted graph. DFS uses recursion or a stack, finishing one branch before another. DFS supports cycle detection and topological order for directed acyclic graphs. Using adjacency lists, both inspect vertices and edges in \(O(V+E)\); mark vertices when enqueued to avoid duplicate expansion.

sections.title: MST algorithms
sections.body: For a connected undirected weighted graph, a spanning tree has V−1 edges. Kruskal sorts edges by weight and uses disjoint sets to reject cycles. Prim grows one tree by repeatedly adding a cheapest edge leaving its current vertex set. The cut property justifies these choices. Disconnected input produces a minimum spanning forest rather than one spanning tree.

sections.title: Weighted shortest paths
sections.body: Dijkstra finalizes the smallest tentative distance and requires nonnegative weights for that greedy argument. Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge repeatedly and detects a reachable negative cycle via further improvement after V−1 rounds. Floyd–Warshall permits intermediate vertices one by one and runs O(V³) for all pairs. Relaxation tests whether dist[u]+w(u,v) improves dist[v].

sections.title: Choose by the property you must preserve
sections.body: An algorithm’s invariant describes what remains true after each operation. Reachability traversal maintains a discovered set; shortest-path algorithms maintain distance estimates; MST algorithms maintain an acyclic set that can still be extended to an optimum. These are different objects even when they all store parent pointers. First translate the requested answer: “fewest hops” is unweighted distance, “minimum total cable” is a spanning-tree objective, and “prerequisites before a task” is a topological-order objective. Then test assumptions: a directed graph needs directed reachability, a disconnected undirected graph has a spanning forest rather than one spanning tree, and topological order requires a DAG. Complexity must include initialization and neighbor enumeration. With lists, summing degrees counts each directed edge once or each undirected edge twice; with a matrix, nonexistent edges still occupy positions to inspect.

lessons.title: BFS, DFS, cycles and topological ordering
lessons.intuition: A traversal marks each vertex once but chooses a different order for the frontier. BFS explores by distance in edges; DFS explores one path and then backtracks. That order determines what additional information you can safely infer.

sections.title: BFS levels
sections.body: Start source distance at zero, mark it visited and enqueue it. Remove a vertex, then discover its unvisited outgoing neighbours with distance one greater. Mark when enqueuing, not only on dequeue, to prevent repeated queued copies. Inductively, all distance-k vertices are processed before distance-(k+1) vertices, so first discovery gives minimum edge count in an unweighted graph.

sections.title: DFS structure
sections.body: Record a vertex as active on entry and finished on exit. A directed edge to an active ancestor is a back edge and proves a cycle. In an undirected graph, the edge back to the DFS parent is not by itself a cycle. DFS trees depend on start vertex and neighbour order, but reachability does not.

sections.title: Topological order
sections.body: A directed acyclic graph has an ordering putting every edge source before its destination. Reverse DFS finishing order gives one after confirming acyclicity. Alternatively Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes zero-indegree vertices. If fewer than V vertices are removed, a cycle remains. Multiple valid topological orders may exist.

sections.title: Why traversal order proves useful facts
sections.body: BFS’s queue places newly discovered vertices after all already queued vertices. If a vertex at distance k is removed, its undiscovered neighbors are assigned distance k+1, while all shorter layers have already had a chance to discover them. That gives a shortest-number-of-edges proof, not just an implementation rule. Marking at enqueue time prevents several parents from adding the same vertex repeatedly. DFS instead keeps a chain of active ancestors. In a directed graph, an edge back to that chain closes a directed cycle; an edge to a completed vertex need not. Finishing a vertex means every recursively reachable unfinished dependency has been processed, which explains why reverse finish order is topological for a DAG. Neighbor order can change parent trees and timestamps without changing reachability or BFS distances.

examples.prompt: BFS on edges A–B,A–C,B–D,C–D from A

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Enqueue A at distance 0; discover B,C at distance 1. Mark each vertex when it is first enqueued, preventing multiple pending copies through different neighbors.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Processing B discovers D at distance 2; mark it immediately. The queue keeps earlier layers ahead of later layers. Neighbor order may change parent choices within the same layer.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Processing C does not reenqueue D. A shortest A-to-D route uses 2 edges. An assigned BFS distance counts edges from the source. This interpretation requires an unweighted or unit-weight objective.

examples.strategy: Use the queue’s first-in-first-out order to expose distance layers.
examples.answer: Processing C does not reenqueue D. A shortest A-to-D route uses 2 edges.
examples.verification: Each discovered vertex’s distance is one more than its parent’s distance; already visited neighbors should not be re-enqueued.

steps: A and B initially have indegree zero.
Remove them in either order; only then does C become available.
Remove C, then D. A,B,C,D and B,A,C,D are both valid.

pitfalls: BFS edge-count shortest paths do not solve arbitrary weighted paths.
In an undirected DFS, skip the parent edge in cycle detection.
revision: Reverse finish order topologically sorts a DAG.

checks.hint: D is discovered from a distance-1 neighbour.
checks.explanation: \(A\to B\)→D or \(A\to C\)→D uses two edges.

checks.hint: Only the relative order of A and B is free.
checks.explanation: The orders are A,B,C,D and B,A,C,D, so 2.

lessons.concept: A traversal marks each vertex once but chooses a different order for the frontier. BFS explores by distance in edges; DFS explores one path and then backtracks. That order determines what additional information you can safely infer.
lessons.method: Start source distance at zero, mark it visited and enqueue it. Remove a vertex, then discover its unvisited outgoing neighbours with distance one greater. Mark when enqueuing, not only on dequeue, to prevent repeated queued copies. Inductively, all distance-k vertices are processed before distance-(k+1) vertices, so first discovery gives minimum edge count in an unweighted graph. Record a vertex as active on entry and finished on exit. A directed edge to an active ancestor is a back edge and proves a cycle. In an undirected graph, the edge back to the DFS parent is not by itself a cycle. DFS trees depend on start vertex and neighbour order, but reachability does not. A directed acyclic graph has an ordering putting every edge source before its destination. Reverse DFS finishing order gives one after confirming acyclicity. Alternatively Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes zero-indegree vertices. If fewer than V vertices are removed, a cycle remains. Multiple valid topological orders may exist. BFS’s queue places newly discovered vertices after all already queued vertices. If a vertex at distance k is removed, its undiscovered neighbors are assigned distance k+1, while all shorter layers have already had a chance to discover them. That gives a shortest-number-of-edges proof, not just an implementation rule. Marking at enqueue time prevents several parents from adding the same vertex repeatedly. DFS instead keeps a chain of active ancestors. In a directed graph, an edge back to that chain closes a directed cycle; an edge to a completed vertex need not. Finishing a vertex means every recursively reachable unfinished dependency has been processed, which explains why reverse finish order is topological for a DAG. Neighbor order can change parent trees and timestamps without changing reachability or BFS distances.

lessons.title: Minimum spanning trees: cuts, Kruskal and Prim
lessons.prerequisite: Weighted undirected graphs and greedy proofs.
lessons.intuition: An MST connects every vertex with minimum total edge weight and no cycles. It is a global network-design objective. The cut property gives a safe local choice and makes greedy algorithms possible.

sections.title: Cut and cycle properties
sections.body: A cut partitions vertices into two nonempty sets; a crossing edge joins the sides. A lightest crossing edge is safe for some MST compatible with current choices under the standard cut argument. If it is uniquely lightest, it belongs to every MST. A uniquely heaviest edge on a cycle cannot belong to any MST. Equal weights require care: several trees may have equal optimal total weight.

sections.title: Kruskal
sections.body: Sort all edges increasingly. Maintain a disjoint-set structure for chosen components. Add an edge if its endpoints are in different components and union them; otherwise reject the cycle-closing edge. Stop at V−1 chosen edges for connected input. Sorting usually dominates at O(E log E).

sections.title: Prim
sections.body: Start at any vertex and repeatedly pick a cheapest edge connecting the current tree to an outside vertex. Maintain best connection keys using a priority queue. This resembles Dijkstra operationally but keys represent cheapest incident attachment, not full source distance. With a binary heap and adjacency lists, a common bound is O(E log V).

sections.title: Exchange arguments behind cut and cycle rules
sections.body: Consider a cut and a lightest edge e crossing it. If an MST does not contain e, adding e creates a cycle; that cycle contains another crossing edge f. Because e is no heavier than f, replacing f by e preserves or improves total weight, so some MST includes e. If e is uniquely lightest, omitting it would force a strictly worse replacement, making it compulsory. Dually, a uniquely heaviest edge on a cycle cannot belong to an MST: deleting it after adding another cycle edge yields a lighter tree. Equality matters. These arguments justify Kruskal’s component merging and Prim’s growing cut. Negative edge weights do not invalidate either algorithm; cycles, connectivity and the total-weight objective matter, rather than the nonnegative-weight restriction used by Dijkstra.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Take AB then BC, connecting A,B,C. The graph and edge weights determine the candidate ordering; equal weights can permit multiple valid choices.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Reject AC because it closes a cycle within that component. Joining separate components preserves acyclicity. Reject an edge whose endpoints are already connected by chosen edges.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Take CD to attach D. Three selected edges total 1+2+4=7. A connected V-vertex tree must have V−1 edges. Sum accepted weights rather than the weights of all inspected edges.

examples.strategy: Accept edges in increasing weight only when they join different components.
examples.answer: Take CD to attach D. Three selected edges total 1+2+4=7.
examples.verification: Chosen edges must connect all vertices and contain no cycle; compare the total with the original weights, not a shortest-path distance.

Removing it still leaves the triangle vertices connectable.

lessons.title: Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall
lessons.prerequisite: Graph relaxation, heaps and dynamic programming.
lessons.intuition: Shortest-path algorithms differ mainly in how they schedule relaxation and which edge weights their proofs tolerate. Treat unreachable distances as infinity and preserve path predecessors if you need a route rather than just its cost.

sections.title: Dijkstra finalization
sections.body: Initialize source to 0 and others to infinity. Extract the unfinalized minimum tentative distance, then relax its outgoing edges. Nonnegative edges ensure no later route through a farther vertex can improve the finalized vertex. A reachable negative edge breaks that proof. Zero weights are allowed. Binary-heap adjacency-list implementations commonly take O((V+E)log V).

sections.title: Bellman–Ford
sections.body: Relax all edges up to V−1 rounds. After round k, shortest paths using at most k edges have been accounted for in the standard formulation. A simple shortest path uses at most V−1 edges when no reachable negative cycle improves it. Another improving pass identifies a reachable negative cycle; not every negative edge is a negative cycle.

sections.title: Floyd–Warshall
sections.body: Let Dᵏ[i,j] allow internal vertices only from the first k. Transition is min(Dᵏ⁻¹[i,j],Dᵏ⁻¹[i,k]+Dᵏ⁻¹[k,j]). It either avoids k or routes through k. Use k as the outer loop in the ordinary in-place implementation, with O(V³) time and \(O(V^2)\) storage. Negative diagonal values after completion detect relevant negative cycles.

sections.title: Why relaxation and finalization differ
sections.body: An actual source-to-vertex walk supplies an upper bound on the shortest distance. Relaxation improves that bound when a route through another vertex is cheaper. Dijkstra finalizes the least tentative vertex because, with nonnegative edges, any unprocessed detour cannot later yield a cheaper entrance to it. A negative edge breaks that proof even without a cycle. Bellman–Ford avoids premature finalization: after k full passes, distances are correct for shortest paths that need at most k edges, assuming each pass considers all edges. Without a reachable negative cycle, a shortest simple path uses at most V−1 edges. An improvement on the next pass therefore signals a reachable negative cycle. A DAG needs neither nonnegative weights nor repeated passes: topological order settles every predecessor before its outgoing relaxation.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: After processing A, tentative B=2,C=7. These first estimates are route costs through A; they remain tentative until the corresponding vertex is finalized.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Finalize B next and relax BC to obtain C=3. B’s distance 2 plus edge BC of weight 1 improves C’s former estimate 7 to 3. Relaxation keeps the cheaper candidate.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Finalize C at 3; predecessor route is A,B,C. Nonnegative weights justify finalization. The predecessor of C is updated to B when the improved route is selected.

examples.strategy: Finalize the smallest tentative distance, then relax its outgoing edges.
examples.answer: Finalize C at 3; predecessor route is A,B,C.
examples.verification: The route \(A\to B\)→C costs 2+1=3, less than direct \(A\to C\) cost 7. Distances never increase under relaxation.

examples.prompt: A negative edge defeating naive Dijkstra
steps: Edges \(A\to B\)=1,\(A\to C\)=2,C→B=−3.
Finalizing B at 1 before C would appear safe under the nonnegative proof.
But \(A\to C\)→B costs −1. Bellman–Ford can discover that improvement; usual Dijkstra assumptions fail.

Only reachable negative cycles affect a single-source problem.

Floyd–Warshall outer loop is intermediate vertex.

lessons.title: Finite automata and regular expressions
lessons.intuition: Finite automata remember only which state they are in. A state should summarize exactly the past information needed to decide future acceptance. This viewpoint is more useful than memorizing transition drawings: design the meaning of states before adding edges.

sections.title: DFA and NFA semantics
sections.body: A DFA has a total transition function Q×Σ→Q, one start state and a set of accepting states. Read the entire string before deciding acceptance. An NFA may have multiple possible transitions and epsilon moves; it accepts if at least one complete path ends accepting. Epsilon moves consume no symbol. Both models recognize exactly regular languages.

sections.title: Subset construction
sections.body: A DFA state can represent a set of possible NFA states. Start with the epsilon closure of the NFA start. For a symbol, take all corresponding moves and then epsilon closure again. A subset is accepting if it contains an accepting NFA state. Up to 2ⁿ subsets exist for n NFA states, but many may be unreachable.

sections.title: Expressions and minimization
sections.body: Regular expressions use union, concatenation and Kleene star; star includes the empty string. Precedence usually places star above concatenation above union. To minimize a DFA, remove unreachable states and distinguish accepting from nonaccepting states, then refine classes when transitions lead to different classes. States are equivalent only if no suffix distinguishes their acceptance.

sections.title: What state equivalence actually means
sections.body: Two DFA states are equivalent when every possible remaining suffix leads either both to acceptance or both to rejection. Agreement on the next symbol alone is insufficient. Start by separating final from nonfinal states because the empty suffix already distinguishes them. Refine a block when members transition, under some symbol, into different blocks; repeating until stable captures longer distinguishing suffixes. Unreachable states do not affect the accepted language and should be removed when minimizing a reachable machine. In a subset DFA, a set is an information state: after reading the prefix, the NFA could be in any member. The empty subset is a valid rejecting sink, not an error. A final member makes the subset accepting because NFA acceptance is existential.

examples.prompt: Design a DFA for an even number of 1s over {0,1}

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Use E and O to remember parity; start in E and accept E. The empty input has zero ones, so the start state must be both even and accepting.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: On 0, stay in the same state because parity does not change. Appending zero preserves the count of ones; keeping the state establishes the parity invariant.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: On 1, toggle E↔O. The empty string is accepted because zero is even. Appending one flips the count’s parity exactly once. Acceptance after the whole input then corresponds to even parity.

examples.strategy: Give each state a meaning that the transition rules preserve.
examples.answer: On 1, toggle E↔O. The empty string is accepted because zero is even.
examples.verification: Trace ε, 0, 1, 11 and 101: their parity results agree with the state meanings, without counting the number of zeros.

steps: The starred prefix permits any binary string, including empty.
The final symbols are specifically 0 then 1.
The expression accepts exactly strings ending in 01, including 01 itself, but not 010.

revision: DFA and NFA have equal expressive power.

lessons.title: Regular languages, closure and pumping lemma
lessons.intuition: The pumping lemma captures a consequence of finite memory: a sufficiently long accepted run repeats a state, creating a loop. It is mainly a tool for proving nonregularity. The order of choices matters because you do not control how the opponent decomposes the string.

sections.title: Regular closure
sections.body: Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation and star. Intersection can be recognized by a product automaton whose states pair the two machines' states. Complement requires a total DFA and flips accepting states. Closure can prove nonregularity indirectly by isolating a known difficult sublanguage.

sections.title: Pumping statement
sections.body: If L is regular, some p exists so every w∈L with |w|≥p can be split w=xyz with \(|xy|\le p\), \(|y|>0\), and xyⁱz∈L for all integers i≥0. The repeated DFA segment is y. This is a necessary condition; merely finding pumpable decompositions does not establish regularity.

sections.title: Proof strategy
sections.body: Assume regularity and let the opponent choose p. Choose a suitable w depending on p. Then handle every valid decomposition, not only one convenient y. Select an exponent i, often 0 or 2, that forces the pumped string out of L. Contradiction disproves the assumed regularity.

sections.title: Quantifiers and closure as proof tools
sections.body: A regular language has a finite-state machine. Reading a sufficiently long accepted word forces a repeated state in an early prefix; the intervening nonempty loop can be repeated or skipped while leaving the remainder’s acceptance unchanged. This explains the length and nonempty constraints of the pumping lemma. It also explains why the proof adversary selects the legal loop: a nonregularity argument must defeat every permitted decomposition. Sometimes closure gives a shorter proof. If an assumed regular L, intersected with a known regular filter, becomes a known nonregular language, the assumption contradicts closure under intersection. To prove regularity, provide a finite automaton, regular expression or sound closure construction. The absence of an obvious pumping counterexample is not such a construction.

steps.title: Accept the adversary’s pumping length
steps.explanation: p is arbitrary; we choose w after p is given. Choosing a fixed short string would not cover all possible pumping lengths.

steps.title: Constrain every legal split
steps.explanation: The entire prefix xy lies in the first p zeros. This covers all legal decompositions, rather than selecting a convenient one.

steps.title: Pump down and contradict membership
steps.explanation: Removing at least one zero leaves unequal counts. The regular pumping lemma requires every nonnegative exponent to remain in L for some legal split, and no split can satisfy that.

examples.given: Language L=\(\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}\).
examples.goal: Prove L is not regular.
examples.strategy: Assume regularity and defeat every permitted split of a carefully chosen word.
examples.answer: L is not regular.
examples.verification: The contradiction uses both \(|xy|\le p\) and \(|y|>0\). Forgetting either constraint would allow decompositions that the proof has not ruled out.

lessons.title: Context-free grammars, derivations and pushdown automata
lessons.intuition: A stack lets a machine remember arbitrarily many pending obligations in last-in-first-out order. Context-free grammars describe recursive structure, and pushdown automata recognize the same language class. Nested parentheses and matched counts are natural examples.

sections.title: Grammar mechanics
sections.body: A CFG has variables, terminals, a start variable and productions whose left side is one variable. Derivation replaces a variable using a production. A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost variable; rightmost expands the rightmost. A parse tree records hierarchical structure, not the temporal order of independent expansions.

sections.title: PDA operation
sections.body: A pushdown automaton chooses transitions using the current state, input symbol or epsilon, and stack top. For 0ⁿ1ⁿ, push one marker per 0, then pop one per 1 and accept when input and markers are exhausted. It must prevent returning to the zero phase after ones begin. Nondeterministic PDAs recognize all CFLs; deterministic PDAs recognize a proper subclass.

sections.title: Ambiguity and closure
sections.body: A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two distinct parse trees, equivalently distinct leftmost derivations. A grammar can be changed while preserving its language. CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star, and under intersection with a regular language; they are not closed under arbitrary intersection or complement.

sections.title: Stack discipline and parse structure
sections.body: A pushdown automaton can store an unbounded count or a nested obligation on its stack. For equal blocks, push once per first-block symbol and pop once per second-block symbol; reject an unmatched pop or remaining unmatched symbols at acceptance. Finite control records the phase so a first-block symbol cannot appear after the second block has begun. A grammar describes the same dependency by recursive nesting: each expansion adds matched symbols around a smaller instance. Ambiguity is about two structures for one terminal string, not simply two different orders of expanding independent branches. Expression grammars use separate nonterminals for precedence levels and recursion direction for associativity. Neither left-recursion removal nor left factoring alone establishes that a grammar is unambiguous or LL(1).

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Start S and apply 0S1 to get 0S1. The recursive production contributes one leading zero and one trailing one, with S representing the unfinished interior.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Apply again to get 00S11. A second recursive expansion nests another matched pair; the terminals remain in zero-then-one block order.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Use S→ε to obtain 0011; each recursive expansion adds a matching outer zero and one. The epsilon production removes only S, not its surrounding terminals. This completes the terminal string.

examples.strategy: Record each sentential form and the production applied to its remaining nonterminal.
examples.answer: Use S→ε to obtain 0011; each recursive expansion adds a matching outer zero and one.
examples.verification: Two recursive expansions yield two zeros and two ones; the resulting 0011 is exactly the target string.

lessons.title: The context-free pumping lemma
lessons.intuition: Context-free pumping repeats two pieces because recursive grammar structure can surround a nested derivation. The proof pattern resembles regular pumping, but its decomposition has five parts and the two pumped parts may be separated.

sections.title: Statement and constraints
sections.body: For a context-free language L, there exists p so every w∈L of length at least p can be written uvxyz with |vxy|≤p, \(|vy|>0\), and uvⁱxyⁱz∈L for all i≥0. At least one of v,y is nonempty; neither individually must be nonempty. The bounded window vxy is important for controlling which symbol blocks can be changed.

sections.title: Proving non-CFL status
sections.body: Assume L is context free, let p be arbitrary, and select a string depending on p. Show every valid decomposition fails for some pumping exponent. Often choose a string with three synchronized blocks so the bounded window cannot alter all required counts together. If pumping disturbs symbol ordering, the string also leaves the language.

sections.title: Limits of the method
sections.body: Failure to find a useful contradiction is not a proof that a language is context free. Establish membership by constructing a grammar or PDA. Closure can simplify a difficult proof: intersecting with a regular language restricts patterns without leaving the CFL class if the original language truly is CFL.

sections.title: The bounded window and legal closure reasoning
sections.body: A sufficiently tall CFG parse tree repeats a nonterminal on one root-to-leaf path. Replacing the larger repeated subtree by the smaller one, or nesting it again, removes or repeats material on two sides of the inner subtree. That is why two substrings are pumped with the same exponent. The bounded window limits where those changes can occur; it is not a bound on the entire word. For three equal separated blocks, a window of length at most p cannot include a symbol from the first and third blocks when the middle block already has length p. Pumping must alter at least one count while leaving another unchanged, or ruin block ordering. CFL closure under intersection with regular languages can isolate a difficult pattern, but intersection with arbitrary CFLs cannot be assumed.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Choose aᵖbᵖcᵖ after the supposed pumping length p. The witness depends on p and belongs to the language. The three blocks each have p symbols, creating separated dependencies.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: The window vxy has length at most p, so it cannot span all three symbol blocks; pumping changes at most two block counts. Any window containing a symbol of both the first and third blocks would include all p middle symbols and exceed length p.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Because \(|vy|>0\), i=0 removes some symbols while one block remains unchanged, or disrupts block order. Either way equal counts/order fail. At least one pumped part is nonempty. Removing it changes some count while at least one untouched block remains length p.

examples.strategy: Cover all legal pumping windows, not one chosen decomposition.
examples.answer: Because \(|vy|>0\), i=0 removes some symbols while one block remains unchanged, or disrupts block order. Either way equal counts/order fail.
examples.verification: Handle boundary-straddling windows as well as single-block windows; even when two counts change equally, the third unchanged count breaks equality.

It cannot be used, regardless of x.
A split with v empty and y nonempty can be valid if the window bound holds.

Both v and y are pumped by the same exponent.

The lemma is a necessary property, not a membership algorithm.

lessons.title: Turing machines and undecidability
lessons.prerequisite: Automata, proof by contradiction and algorithms.
lessons.intuition: A Turing machine adds an unbounded writable tape to finite control. It models general algorithmic computation. The crucial distinction is whether a machine always halts with an answer or may run forever on some negative instances.

sections.title: Deciders and recognizers
sections.body: A decider halts on every input and accepts exactly its language. A recognizer accepts members but may reject or loop on nonmembers. Every decidable language is recognizable, but not conversely. If both a language and its complement have recognizers, interleave their steps; one must accept, giving a decider.

sections.title: The halting contradiction
sections.body: Suppose H can decide whether any machine halts on an input. Construct D that on machine code x loops if H says machine x halts on x, and halts otherwise. Running D on its own code makes either prediction contradict what D does. Thus no general halting decider exists.

sections.title: Reductions and Rice
sections.body: To show B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable A to B: transform A instances computably so a hypothetical B decider would decide A. Reversing the reduction proves the wrong implication. Rice’s theorem states every nontrivial property of the language recognized by a machine is undecidable; syntactic facts such as the number of states are not such semantic properties.

sections.title: Halting guarantees and reduction direction
sections.body: A recognizer must eventually accept members but can reject or loop on nonmembers. A decider must halt with the correct result on both kinds of input. Complementing a recognizer by flipping its accepting and rejecting states does not fix infinite loops; complementing a decider does work. If both a language and its complement have recognizers, alternating one step of each produces a decider because exactly one eventually accepts. For an undecidability reduction, suppose a solver for your target problem exists and show how it would solve a known impossible problem. The input transformation must itself halt and preserve yes/no membership in the stated direction. Rice’s theorem concerns nontrivial semantic properties of recognized languages, not arbitrary syntactic questions such as the number of states written in a machine description.

examples.prompt: Turn two recognizers into a decider

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Run one recognizer for L and one for its complement in alternating steps on the same input. Use separate saved machine configurations and alternate their steps; both simulations receive unbounded progress.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: If the first accepts, answer yes; if the second accepts, answer no. The recognizer for the correct side eventually accepts, so its answer determines membership without needing the other to halt.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Every input belongs to exactly one side, so some recognizer eventually accepts. Running one to completion first could loop forever. Exactly one side contains any given input. This supplies the termination proof that each recognizer alone lacks.

examples.strategy: Interleave simulations to avoid waiting forever for one recognizer to reject.
examples.answer: Every input belongs to exactly one side, so some recognizer eventually accepts. Running one to completion first could loop forever.
examples.verification: For a member, the L simulation accepts; for a nonmember, the complement simulation accepts. Both cases terminate under dovetailing.

steps: Assume a computable transform maps x∈A iff f(x)∈B.
If B had a decider, first compute f(x), then call it and return the same answer.
That would decide A. If A is undecidable, B cannot have such a decider.

pitfalls: Recognizable does not mean decidable.
Reduction direction is essential.
Rice applies to semantic language properties, not all machine properties.
revision: Decider halts everywhere; recognizer need not.
Known hard A≤B establishes hardness of B.

checks.hint: Consider negative instances.

name: Compiler Design
description: Follow a program from source to execution

lessons.title: Lexical analysis and tokenization
lessons.intuition: The lexer groups characters into meaningful token classes before the parser checks grammar structure. A token records a category and possibly an attribute, while the lexeme is the actual source substring. Separating them lets a grammar treat every identifier similarly.

sections.title: Token definitions
sections.body: Identifiers, keywords, numeric literals, operators and punctuation are common token classes. Regular expressions describe many lexical patterns; automata implement them. Whitespace and comments may be discarded or retained as metadata depending on the language. Symbol-table entries link identifier tokens to later declaration/type information.

sections.title: Longest match and priority
sections.body: At each input position, a lexer typically chooses the longest matching lexeme. When matches have equal length, a rule priority resolves the tie, often recognizing a keyword before a generic identifier. Thus >= is one token rather than > followed by = if the token rule allows it. A keyword prefix inside an identifier does not force splitting: whilex can remain an identifier.

sections.title: Errors and boundaries
sections.body: A lexical error is an unrecognized character sequence under the token rules. A valid token sequence can still have a parse error, such as misplaced parentheses. Nested structure is ordinarily handled by the parser, not by ordinary finite-automaton token rules. Scanner buffering must preserve character positions and handle end-of-input correctly.

sections.title: How longest match is implemented
sections.body: A lexer can continue a DFA scan while remembering the most recent accepting position and the corresponding highest-priority rule. When no transition is possible, it returns to that remembered position and emits the token. This separates longest match from tie resolution. For an identifier rule accepting letters followed by letters or digits, “ifx” has a longer identifier match than the keyword “if”; “if” alone can use keyword priority because both matches have equal length. The lexeme is the actual character slice; the token kind is its category; an attribute may hold a numeric value or symbol-table index. Syntax nesting such as arbitrarily balanced parentheses belongs to parsing, since finite-state token recognition has no unbounded stack.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: sum is an identifier, = an assignment operator, and a another identifier. The two identifiers are different lexemes but belong to the same token kind. Spaces separate text but are not emitted here.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: + is an arithmetic operator, 12 a numeric literal, and ; punctuation. The numeric literal is one token despite containing two digits; punctuation also contributes a token.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: There are 6 tokens if whitespace is ignored; lexemes differ from their category names. Count emitted tokens rather than characters or distinct categories. A repeated category still creates a new token occurrence.

lessons.title: Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW and LL/LR methods
lessons.intuition: A parser discovers grammatical structure in a token stream. Predictive parsing chooses productions before seeing their full result; bottom-up parsing recognizes handles after seeing the right-hand side. FIRST and FOLLOW sets summarize where grammar decisions can be made.

sections.title: FIRST and FOLLOW
sections.body: FIRST(α) contains terminals that can begin a string derived from α, plus ε if α can disappear. For a sequence, continue into later symbols when earlier ones are nullable. FOLLOW(A) contains terminals that can follow A in some sentential form; the start symbol includes end marker $. For A→αBβ, add FIRST(β) without ε to FOLLOW(B), and if β is nullable add FOLLOW(A).

sections.title: LL(1) prediction
sections.body: For A→α, put the production under terminals in FIRST(α); if α is nullable, also under FOLLOW(A). A conflict means the grammar is not LL(1) as written. Eliminate direct left recursion and factor common prefixes when appropriate, without assuming those changes fix every grammar. Recursive descent expands a leftmost derivation.

sections.title: Bottom-up parsing
sections.body: An LR parser tracks states representing viable prefixes, shifts input symbols and reduces a recognized right-hand side to its left-hand variable. Reductions reconstruct a rightmost derivation in reverse. Shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts signal ambiguity or insufficient parsing information for the chosen method. LR handles a wider grammar class than LL(1).

sections.title: Deriving predictive choices and LR conflicts
sections.body: FIRST records terminals that can begin a derivation, whereas FOLLOW records terminals that can legally come immediately after a nonterminal in a sentential form. If a production’s right side can vanish, the parser must choose it when the lookahead belongs to the left side’s FOLLOW set. This is why nullable prefixes propagate FIRST from later symbols. Compute these sets repeatedly until no change; a single left-to-right sweep can miss indirect dependencies. LL(1) fails when two productions demand the same table cell. LR item sets instead encode how far productions have been recognized. An LR(0) completed item proposes a reduction independent of lookahead; SLR restricts reductions using FOLLOW; LR(1) items carry their own lookaheads. A shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict must be assessed for that specific table construction.

For A→α, put the production under terminals in FIRST(α); if α is nullable, also under FOLLOW(A). A conflict means the grammar is not LL(1) as written. Eliminate direct left recursion and factor common prefixes when appropriate, without assuming those changes fix every grammar. Recursive descent expands a leftmost derivation. An LR parser tracks states representing viable prefixes, shifts input symbols and reduces a recognized right-hand side to its left-hand variable. Reductions reconstruct a rightmost derivation in reverse. Shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts signal ambiguity or insufficient parsing information for the chosen method. LR handles a wider grammar class than LL(1). FIRST records terminals that can begin a derivation, whereas FOLLOW records terminals that can legally come immediately after a nonterminal in a sentential form. If a production’s right side can vanish, the parser must choose it when the lookahead belongs to the left side’s FOLLOW set. This is why nullable prefixes propagate FIRST from later symbols. Compute these sets repeatedly until no change; a single left-to-right sweep can miss indirect dependencies. LL(1) fails when two productions demand the same table cell. LR item sets instead encode how far productions have been recognized. An LR(0) completed item proposes a reduction independent of lookahead; SLR restricts reductions using FOLLOW; LR(1) items carry their own lookaheads. A shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict must be assessed for that specific table construction.
lessons.example: For S→Ab and A→a|ε, compute FIRST(S)

gateGuide.recognize: Predictive parsing uses FIRST/FOLLOW; LR parsing uses viable prefixes and item states. Label the parser family before building a table.
method: Compute nullable symbols first, then FIRST and FOLLOW to a fixed point.
For A→α place it under FIRST(α) terminals; if α is nullable also use FOLLOW(A).
For LR trace closure/goto and the stated lookahead rules; identify the exact cell with multiple actions.

traps.claim: FIRST(AB) is always FIRST(A)
traps.why: If A is nullable, terminals from FIRST(B) also matter.

traps.claim: An unambiguous grammar is always LL(1)
traps.why: Left-recursive unambiguous expression grammars still fail predictive parsing; ambiguity and parser suitability are different properties.

formulas.meaning: Nullable α additionally uses FOLLOW(A).
End marker follows the start symbol.

lessons.title: Syntax-directed translation and runtime environments
lessons.intuition: A parse tree can carry semantic information such as expression values or types. Syntax-directed translation describes how this information moves. Runtime environments then arrange the storage needed when the translated program actually executes.

sections.title: Attributes and evaluation
sections.body: Synthesized attributes are computed from children and flow upward; inherited attributes receive information from a parent or relevant siblings. Semantic rules define dependencies, and a legal evaluation order respects that dependency graph. S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit bottom-up evaluation naturally. L-attributed definitions restrict inherited dependencies for left-to-right evaluation.

sections.title: Translation actions
sections.body: An annotated syntax tree can compute expression types, values, offsets or emitted code. For E→E₁+T, a synthesized value rule may set E.val=E₁.val+T.val. Translation schemes embed actions in productions, so action placement determines execution order during a derivation. Parsing correctness alone does not guarantee the semantic actions are correct.

sections.title: Runtime storage
sections.body: An activation record can include arguments, return address, saved registers, locals and links. A dynamic link points to the caller’s frame; a static link supports lexical nesting and can point somewhere different. Stack allocation supports ordinary call-return lifetimes; heap allocation supports objects that outlive their creating call. Recursion needs separate frames even for the same function.

sections.title: Dependency graphs and environment links
sections.body: Attribute evaluation is a scheduling problem: each attribute value must be computed after the values it depends on. Synthesized attributes flow from child computations to a parent. Inherited attributes can flow from the parent or permitted siblings; not every inherited definition can be evaluated in a single left-to-right traversal. A cycle in the dependency graph prevents a simple evaluation order. At runtime, each call creates an activation record containing its own parameters, locals and return information under the calling convention. The dynamic link follows the chain of callers; the static link follows lexical nesting for nonlocal variable access. Recursive calls share the same source-level procedure but require distinct live records. Returning restores the caller’s execution context rather than reinitializing it.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The multiplication node synthesizes 3×4=12. The multiplication subtree is evaluated before its parent addition, because the parse groups 3*4 together.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: The addition node receives child values 2 and 12. The child attribute values are inputs to the addition node’s synthesized attribute.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: It synthesizes 14; using a different parse tree could produce a different arithmetic order. The result belongs to this parse tree. Evaluating source tokens left-to-right without precedence would incorrectly give 20.

examples.strategy: Evaluate child attributes after the parse structure fixes operator precedence.
examples.answer: It synthesizes 14; using a different parse tree could produce a different arithmetic order.
examples.verification: Independent arithmetic 2+(3×4)=14 agrees. If the grammar were ambiguous, the tree would need to be specified first.

steps: main owns one frame; first f creates another.
Recursive f creates a third frame with its own locals.
Returning from inner f releases only its frame and restores the caller f’s state.

pitfalls: Static and dynamic links serve different relationships.
Same function code does not imply shared local variables.
revision: Synthesized flows upward; inherited receives context.
Activation records represent invocations, not functions as unique objects.

checks.prompt: For the parse tree 2+(3*4), what value is synthesized at the root?
checks.hint: Evaluate the multiplication child first.

checks.prompt: main calls f, which calls f again. How many frames are active before any return, counting main?
checks.hint: Count invocations rather than distinct names.
checks.explanation: main, outer f and inner f give three frames.

method: Classify each attribute as synthesized or inherited and draw its dependency edges.

traps.claim: Static links always point to the caller
traps.why: They point to the lexically enclosing environment; the caller can be a different procedure.

traps.claim: One variable name means one runtime memory cell

lessons.title: Intermediate code, local optimization and data-flow analysis
lessons.prerequisite: Expressions, CFG control flow and sets.
lessons.intuition: Intermediate representations expose simple operations and control flow so optimizations can reason about program behaviour. An optimization must preserve observable semantics; matching expression text is insufficient when operands may have changed.

sections.title: Three-address code and blocks
sections.body: Break compound expressions into assignments with at most a small fixed number of operands, such as t1=b*c; t2=a+t1. A basic block has one entry and no internal control-flow branch except at its end. Leaders include the first instruction, jump targets and instructions following jumps. A control-flow graph connects blocks by possible transfers.

sections.title: Local optimization
sections.body: Constant folding evaluates constant expressions; constant propagation substitutes known constants. Common-subexpression elimination reuses a previously computed expression only if its operands and relevant memory remain unchanged. Dead-code elimination removes computations whose results have no future use, provided they have no required side effects. Overflow, aliasing and floating-point rules can constrain algebraic transformations.

sections.title: Data flow
sections.body: Liveness is a backward may-analysis: OUT[B]=union of successors' IN sets; IN[B]=USE[B]∪(OUT[B]−DEF[B]). A variable is live if some continuation reads its current value before redefinition. Available expressions use forward propagation and typically intersection at joins because an expression must be available on every incoming path. Iterate finite-set equations to a fixed point.

sections.title: Why a fixed point represents all paths
sections.body: A variable is live at a program point if some path reads its present value before overwriting it. The word “some” makes the merge operator union: an obligation from any successor matters. At block exit, collect live-in sets of successors. Moving backward through the block, definitions kill the old value’s obligation and uses add obligations. Repeating across a loop is necessary because a successor may depend on information that returns through the back edge. In a finite powerset lattice with monotone transfers and the correct initialization, iteration stabilizes. Available expressions use an all-path requirement, so their meet is intersection instead. Common-subexpression elimination must establish operand stability on every relevant path; a potential aliasing write invalidates an otherwise visually repeated expression.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Emit t1=c*d because multiplication occurs first. The product is a prerequisite for addition, so its temporary must be defined first.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Emit t2=b+t1. The addition refers to the already computed product temporary, preserving precedence without parentheses in the IR.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Emit a=t2. The temporaries make dependencies explicit for later analysis. The final copy stores the expression result in a; temporary naming is arbitrary but dependency order is not.

examples.strategy: Emit one three-address operation per expression-tree computation in dependency order.
examples.answer: Emit a=t2. The temporaries make dependencies explicit for later analysis.
examples.verification: Substitute t1=c*d into t2=b+t1 and then into a=t2 to reconstruct a=b+c*d.

examples.prompt: Find live-in when USE={a}, DEF={b}, OUT={b,c}
steps: Remove definitions from OUT: {b,c}−{b}={c}.
Union with USE: {a}∪{c}={a,c}.
Thus b’s old value is not needed on entry, but a and c are.

pitfalls: Reusing a+b after assigning a is invalid without additional proof.
A may-analysis join uses union; must-properties often require intersection.
revision: Preserve side effects when removing dead results.

checks.prompt: Which join is used for live-variable OUT sets at multiple successors?
checks.hint: A variable is live if some future path needs it.
checks.explanation: Liveness is a may-property; union includes variables needed on any successor continuation.

checks.prompt: For t=4; u=t+6, what constant does propagation and folding assign to u?
checks.hint: Substitute t before arithmetic.

method: Write GEN/KILL or USE/DEF for each block from the stated analysis.

traps.why: A reassignment to an operand or an aliased write can invalidate its previous value.

traps.claim: Liveness describes whether a variable has a current value

name: Operating System
description: Processes, memory and the systems between them

lessons.title: System calls, processes, threads and IPC
lessons.intuition: A running program needs an execution context and protected resources. Processes give resource isolation; threads share much of that context while scheduling independently. Kernel entry is controlled because ordinary programs must not directly manipulate every device or other process.

sections.title: System calls and process states
sections.body: A system call enters privileged kernel handling through an architecture-defined trap mechanism. The kernel validates arguments and performs protected work. A process can be running, ready or blocked; blocked means waiting for an event, not merely waiting for CPU. A context switch saves and restores execution state and is distinct from any user-to-kernel mode transition.

sections.title: Threads and creation
sections.body: Threads in one process share an address space and open resources but normally have separate stacks and register contexts. A process creation mechanism such as fork copies a logical process context; modern implementations may initially share pages via copy-on-write. Different processes do not ordinarily share arbitrary writable memory unless explicitly arranged.

sections.title: IPC mechanisms
sections.body: Pipes and message queues move data with OS coordination. Shared memory lets processes access a common region and can reduce copying but requires synchronization. Signals provide notifications rather than general large-data transfer. Blocking calls suspend a caller until conditions are met; nonblocking calls return immediately with status. Choose the mechanism based on data size, synchronization and isolation needs.

sections.title: State changes and independent execution contexts
sections.body: A ready process can execute once given a processor; a blocked process cannot progress until its awaited event occurs. Preemption changes running to ready, while waiting for I/O changes running to blocked. I/O completion generally makes the process ready and does not guarantee immediate execution. Threads of one process commonly share address space, open resources and globals, but have their own registers and stacks. A switch must preserve enough execution context to resume the selected thread correctly. fork conceptually duplicates a process’s execution state and returns different values in parent and child; exec replaces the current program image without creating another process. A blocking system call can trigger a context switch, but a system call that completes immediately need not.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: A process waiting for the scheduler after exhausting a time slice is ready. Its CPU work is executable but it has not been chosen; this is ready, not blocked.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: A process waiting for disk completion is blocked. The required data/event is not available, so assigning CPU alone cannot make the pending operation progress.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: When disk completion arrives, it usually becomes ready before the scheduler runs it again. Event completion removes the blocking condition; scheduling is a separate decision that selects among ready processes.

examples.strategy: Classify a process by what prevents its next instruction from executing.
examples.answer: When disk completion arrives, it usually becomes ready before the scheduler runs it again.
examples.verification: A ready process needs CPU selection; a blocked process needs an event first. These are different waiting queues.

examples.prompt: Two threads modify a shared global
steps: Both threads refer to the same process-global object.
Each still has its own local stack variables and instruction pointer.
Sharing the global creates a synchronization responsibility; having two stacks does not isolate global state.

pitfalls: A mode switch is not necessarily a process switch.
Shared memory does not automatically synchronize access.
revision: Process isolates resources; threads share address space.
Ready waits for CPU; blocked waits for an event.

checks.prompt: Four threads share one process. How many ordinary thread stacks are needed?
checks.hint: Each thread needs its own active call context.
checks.explanation: One stack per thread gives four stacks.

checks.prompt: A single CPU runs one thread at an instant in this simplified model. How many threads can be running simultaneously?
checks.hint: Ignore multicore hardware in the stated model.
checks.explanation: A single execution core runs one thread at a time.
