method: Draw process creation as a tree and track which processes reach each later statement.
List resources that are copied, shared or replaced under the stated API.
For interleavings enforce each thread’s program order and synchronization edges, then enumerate possible outcomes.

traps.claim: Every fork doubles the original process count regardless of control flow
traps.why: Only processes that actually execute that fork create a child; branches and failures change the count.

traps.claim: Context switching and entering kernel mode are identical
traps.why: A system call can enter the kernel and return to the same process without a scheduler switch.

formulas.meaning: k unconditional successful fork calls reached by every existing process, with no early exits.

lessons.title: Concurrency, mutexes and semaphores
lessons.intuition: Concurrency allows operations to overlap in time even on one CPU. If a shared update consists of separate read and write steps, scheduling can interleave those steps and lose information. Correct synchronization constrains interleavings, not just the final line of source code.

sections.title: Race conditions and critical sections
sections.body: A data race involves unsynchronized conflicting accesses under the applicable memory model; broader race conditions make correctness depend on timing. A critical section protects shared invariants. Mutual exclusion ensures at most one entrant, while progress and bounded waiting address liveness. Declaring an object volatile is not a substitute for atomicity or a lock.

sections.title: Mutex and semaphore
sections.body: A mutex gives exclusive ownership around a protected region. A semaphore maintains a count with atomic wait and signal operations. wait decrements when available or blocks; signal returns a permit or wakes a waiter under the implementation model. A binary semaphore can coordinate single access but ownership semantics need not match a mutex. Counting semaphores manage multiple identical resources.

sections.title: Producer–consumer
sections.body: For a capacity-N buffer, use empty=N, full=0 and a mutex for buffer manipulation. Producer waits for empty then locks, inserts, unlocks and signals full; consumer symmetrically waits for full and later signals empty. Waiting for availability while holding the buffer mutex can block the other side from making progress.

sections.title: Proving safety separately from progress
sections.body: An invariant such as “at most one thread is in the critical section” is a safety property: no bad simultaneous access occurs. Progress asks that eligible attempts can eventually enter; bounded waiting strengthens this with a bound on overtaking. A design can be safe and still starve a thread forever. Locking only the write in a read-modify-write operation is insufficient because another thread may change the value after an unprotected read. Protect the whole invariant-preserving update. Condition variables normally wait by atomically releasing the associated lock and sleeping, then reacquire the lock before returning. Recheck the predicate in a loop because wakeups and competing consumers may leave it false. Semaphores store permits, whereas a condition notification does not generally store a future entitlement.

examples.prompt: Show a lost update for shared x=0

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Thread A reads 0; thread B reads 0. Both reads can occur before either write because the compound update is not protected atomically.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: A computes and stores 1; B also computes and stores 1. Each computation uses its own saved read value zero, so both stores write the same one.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Two increments finish with x=1 rather than 2. Locking the whole read-modify-write operation prevents that interleaving. The final store overwrites the same value instead of accumulating both increments. The protected region must include the read.

examples.strategy: Split increment into read, compute and store, then interleave legal events.
examples.answer: Two increments finish with x=1 rather than 2. Locking the whole read-modify-write operation prevents that interleaving.
examples.verification: The interleaving respects each thread’s local order yet ends at 1. Serializing complete increments gives 2, proving the race changes the outcome.

steps: Initialize semaphore count to 3.
Three successful waits consume all permits, leaving 0.
A fourth requester must block until some owner signals, restoring a permit.

pitfalls: Protect the whole invariant update, not only one read or store.
Incorrect lock order can introduce deadlock.
revision: Mutual exclusion protects safety; progress/bounded waiting protect liveness.
Counting semaphore permits model resource capacity.

checks.prompt: A semaphore starts at 5 and three waits succeed without signals. What is its remaining count?
checks.hint: Each successful wait consumes one permit.

checks.prompt: Two correctly locked increments start from x=7. What is the final value?
checks.hint: Both increments take effect serially.

method: Split non-atomic updates into read, compute and write events.
Check mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting independently.

traps.claim: A single source-level increment is atomic
traps.why: Two threads can read the same old value and overwrite each other’s increments.

traps.claim: Mutual exclusion guarantees bounded waiting
traps.why: A lock can prevent simultaneous entry while repeatedly starving one contender.

formulas.meaning: Atomic semaphore operation; implementation conventions for negative counts vary.
A counting semaphore permits multiple concurrent holders when initialized above one.

lessons.title: Deadlock, avoidance and safe states
lessons.intuition: Deadlock is a circular dependency in which participants cannot proceed. A state can be unsafe without already being deadlocked: unsafe means future declared resource demands might prevent a guaranteed completion order.

sections.title: Necessary conditions
sections.body: The standard Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no forced resource preemption and circular wait. All are necessary in the usual resource-allocation model. Prevention deliberately breaks one, for example imposing a global resource-acquisition order to rule out circular waiting.

sections.title: Avoidance with Banker
sections.body: Each process declares its maximum demand. Need=Max−Allocation, and Available is the currently free vector. A safety test repeatedly finds a process with Need≤Work, assumes it completes, and adds its Allocation back to Work. If all can be removed, the resulting sequence certifies safety. A resource request is tentatively granted only if the new state passes the test.

sections.title: Detection and model limits
sections.body: In a single-instance resource graph, a cycle corresponds to deadlock; with multiple instances, a cycle need not be sufficient. Detection examines actual allocations and outstanding requests rather than maximum future claims. Recovery can terminate or roll back processes or preempt suitable resources. Starvation is indefinite denial to a participant while others may still progress, which differs from deadlock.

sections.title: What a safety certificate guarantees
sections.body: A safe state admits an order in which every process can receive its full remaining declared claim, complete and release resources. The safety algorithm does not predict actual scheduling; it constructs a witness that the system could satisfy even worst-case claims. Work is a temporary available-resource vector and must be compared componentwise with Need. Finishing a hypothetical process adds its held allocation to Work, producing a monotone increase. If no unfinished process is feasible, the current state lacks a safety certificate under those maximum claims. That is an unsafe-state finding, not proof that every process is already blocked. Deadlock prevention removes a necessary condition such as circular wait; avoidance uses future-claim information; detection evaluates actual outstanding requests and allocations.

examples.prompt: Check safety: Available=1, P1 allocation=1/max=2, P2 allocation=1/max=3

steps.title: Compute remaining needs
steps.explanation: Maximum claims are totals, not additional requests. Need is the remaining claim after currently held resources.

steps.title: Finish P1 hypothetically
steps.explanation: P1 can receive its remaining resource and complete. In the safety algorithm, adding its original allocation captures the net increase after borrowed Work is returned.

steps.title: Finish P2 hypothetically
steps.explanation: Every process can finish in order P1,P2, so this is a safe sequence. P2 could not have been chosen first at Work=1.

examples.given: One resource type. Available=1; P1 holds 1 with maximum 2; P2 holds 1 with maximum 3.
examples.goal: Determine whether the state is safe.
examples.strategy: Use a private Work variable and find an order of hypothetical completions.
examples.answer: Safe; a safety witness is P1 followed by P2.
examples.verification: Final Work=3 equals total system resources: initial Available 1 plus both original allocations. Adding Max instead would incorrectly create resources.

steps: Every thread must acquire lock A before lock B.
A thread holding B cannot wait for A because that acquisition order is disallowed.
This removes a possible A↔B circular wait, though other correctness concerns still need analysis.

pitfalls: Unsafe is not synonymous with already deadlocked.
A cycle is not sufficient in every multiple-instance resource graph.
revision: Safety test simulates finishing processes and releasing allocations.

checks.prompt: Which statement about an unsafe resource state is correct?
checks.hint: Avoidance reasons about possible future demands.
checks.explanation: Unsafe means no safe sequence under declared maximum demands. Current requests may still permit progress, so actual deadlock is not established.
options: It lacks a guaranteed safe completion sequence but may not be deadlocked yet
It always has zero available resources

lessons.concept: Deadlock is a circular dependency in which participants cannot proceed. A state can be unsafe without already being deadlocked: unsafe means future declared resource demands might prevent a guaranteed completion order.
lessons.method: The standard Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no forced resource preemption and circular wait. All are necessary in the usual resource-allocation model. Prevention deliberately breaks one, for example imposing a global resource-acquisition order to rule out circular waiting. Each process declares its maximum demand. Need=Max−Allocation, and Available is the currently free vector. A safety test repeatedly finds a process with Need≤Work, assumes it completes, and adds its Allocation back to Work. If all can be removed, the resulting sequence certifies safety. A resource request is tentatively granted only if the new state passes the test. In a single-instance resource graph, a cycle corresponds to deadlock; with multiple instances, a cycle need not be sufficient. Detection examines actual allocations and outstanding requests rather than maximum future claims. Recovery can terminate or roll back processes or preempt suitable resources. Starvation is indefinite denial to a participant while others may still progress, which differs from deadlock. A safe state admits an order in which every process can receive its full remaining declared claim, complete and release resources. The safety algorithm does not predict actual scheduling; it constructs a witness that the system could satisfy even worst-case claims. Work is a temporary available-resource vector and must be compared componentwise with Need. Finishing a hypothetical process adds its held allocation to Work, producing a monotone increase. If no unfinished process is feasible, the current state lacks a safety certificate under those maximum claims. That is an unsafe-state finding, not proof that every process is already blocked. Deadlock prevention removes a necessary condition such as circular wait; avoidance uses future-claim information; detection evaluates actual outstanding requests and allocations.

gateGuide.recognize: Deadlock, unsafe state and starvation are distinct. Banker’s safety test uses maximum claims and hypothetical completions.
method: Compute Need=Max−Allocation and copy Available into Work.
Repeatedly find an unfinished process whose Need≤Work, then add its current Allocation to Work.
A complete sequence proves safety; for requests first test request≤Need and request≤Available, simulate and rerun safety.

traps.claim: Unsafe means currently deadlocked
traps.why: An unsafe state lacks a guaranteed safe completion sequence; actual requests may still allow everyone to finish.

traps.claim: A cycle always proves deadlock with multiple instances
traps.why: Cycle sufficiency applies to single-instance resource types; multiple instances require a stronger analysis.

lessons.title: CPU and I/O scheduling
lessons.intuition: Scheduling chooses which waiting work receives a resource next. A schedule should be traced on a time axis using arrival times and preemption rules. Waiting, response and turnaround times describe different experiences and should not be interchanged.

sections.title: CPU metrics
sections.body: Turnaround=completion−arrival. In the single CPU-burst model, waiting=turnaround−burst. Response time measures first execution−arrival. FCFS serves arrival order and may create a convoy behind a long job. Nonpreemptive SJF picks the shortest available next burst; shortest-remaining-time-first is its preemptive variant. Future arrivals cannot be scheduled before they exist.

sections.title: Round-robin
sections.body: Run each ready process for at most quantum q, then requeue if unfinished. Small q improves opportunities for responsiveness but raises context-switch overhead; very large q approaches FCFS. At simultaneous arrivals/completions define the queue tie convention. Priority scheduling may starve low-priority work; aging can increase priority over time.

sections.title: Disk scheduling
sections.body: FCFS follows request order. SSTF picks the nearest requested cylinder, potentially starving distant requests. SCAN moves in a direction and reverses, while LOOK reverses at the last request rather than physical end. C-SCAN serves one direction with a return movement. Total head travel depends on the initial position, direction and whether endpoint movement counts.

sections.title: Use events rather than averaging burst lengths
sections.body: A scheduling decision can occur at an arrival, completion, quantum expiration or blocking event, depending on the policy. In nonpreemptive SJF, a newly arriving shorter job does not displace the running job; SRTF compares remaining time at relevant arrivals. Round robin appends unfinished work to a ready queue at quantum expiry, but arrivals and a simultaneous expiry need an explicitly stated tie convention. Waiting time is accumulated time in the ready queue. For a single CPU-only burst, turnaround equals waiting plus service, which permits subtraction; for workloads with I/O, blocked time must also be accounted for. Response time ends at the first CPU dispatch. Draw a separate timeline for each policy, and calculate per-process values before taking their arithmetic mean.

steps.title: Build the Gantt chart

steps.title: Calculate waiting
steps.explanation: FCFS is nonpreemptive here, so each process waits only before its first execution.

steps.title: Calculate turnaround
steps.explanation: Turnaround includes both waiting and CPU service. It is measured from arrival to completion.

Disk LOOK and SCAN endpoint rules differ.

lessons.title: Memory management, virtual memory and file systems
lessons.intuition: Virtual memory separates a program’s address space from physical placement. A translation may be missing from the TLB even when the page is resident; a page fault instead means the required resident mapping cannot complete normally and OS handling is needed.

sections.title: Paging and translation
sections.body: Split a virtual address into page number and offset. The page table maps the page number to a physical frame; offset is unchanged. A TLB caches translations, not ordinarily the data itself. Page-table size depends on page count and entry size. Larger pages reduce entry count but can increase internal fragmentation. Segmentation models variable-size logical regions and has different allocation trade-offs.

sections.title: Replacement and faults
sections.body: Demand paging loads pages when first needed or after eviction. FIFO removes the oldest loaded page, LRU the least recently used, and optimal the page whose next use is farthest in the future. Optimal needs future knowledge and is a benchmark. FIFO can exhibit Belady’s anomaly; LRU is a stack algorithm and does not. Too few frames for active working sets can cause thrashing.

sections.title: File organization
sections.body: Directories map names to metadata or file identifiers. Contiguous allocation supports simple sequential/random positioning but complicates growth; linked allocation traverses pointers; indexed allocation stores block pointers in an index structure. Free-space maps, access permissions and crash consistency are separate responsibilities. An inode-like record can point to direct and indirect block addresses.

sections.title: Page-table walks and replacement state
sections.body: Paging preserves the offset because a page and its physical frame have equal size. The page-table entry supplies the frame number and permission/residency metadata. A TLB caches recent translations, so a miss can be resolved by an ordinary page-table walk without disk access. A nonresident page is a page fault and invokes a much slower path that can include eviction, dirty-page writeback, load and restart. Replacement policies have distinct state: FIFO records load order, LRU records last reference, and optimal replacement uses the future reference sequence as a comparison benchmark. A hit changes LRU recency but not FIFO age. Compare page faults on the same initial frame state and reference string. Effective access time needs complete mutually exclusive paths; a miss penalty defined as extra time must not have the baseline counted twice.

examples.prompt: Translate virtual address 5000 with 4 KiB pages

steps.title: Convert page size
steps.explanation: The page size determines the offset range 0…4095 and is the same for pages and frames.

steps.title: Split the virtual address
steps.explanation: Quotient identifies the virtual page. Remainder identifies a byte within that page, and must be less than 4096.

steps.title: Substitute the physical frame
steps.explanation: The page table supplies frame 7. Mapping relocates the page but preserves the byte’s offset.

examples.given: Virtual byte address 5000; page size 4 KiB; virtual page 1 maps to frame 7.
examples.goal: Translate to a physical byte address.
examples.strategy: Divide into quotient and remainder, translate only the quotient, preserve the offset.
examples.answer: Physical byte address 29,576.
examples.verification: Dividing 29,576 by 4,096 yields frame 7 and remainder 904, confirming the translation.

steps: 1 faults and loads; 2 faults and loads.
The second reference to 1 hits but does not change FIFO age.
3 faults and evicts 1, the oldest loaded page. Total faults=3; LRU would evict 2 instead.

pitfalls: A TLB miss is not automatically a page fault.
FIFO age is load order, not last access.

lessons.title: File systems, allocation and free-space management
lessons.intuition: A file system connects human names and byte offsets to physical blocks. File metadata, block allocation and directory structure have different responsibilities. A lookup cost depends on which metadata is cached and which indirection levels must be read.

sections.title: Allocation choices
sections.body: Contiguous allocation stores consecutive blocks and computes block location by start+index, but growth and external fragmentation are challenges. Linked allocation stores the next block address in each block or a separate table; random access requires following links unless indexed metadata helps. Indexed allocation keeps a pointer array or tree so a chosen logical block can be located without reading all previous data blocks.

sections.title: Direct and indirect pointers
sections.body: An inode-style record can have several direct pointers, a pointer to one indirect block of addresses, and further levels. If a block has B bytes and an address occupies a bytes, an indirect block holds B/a pointers ignoring metadata. A double-indirect path can cover (B/a)² data blocks. Access cost includes metadata blocks that are not already cached.

sections.title: Directories and consistency
sections.body: Directory entries connect names to file identifiers; hard links can give multiple names for the same file object while symbolic links contain a path to be resolved. Free-space bitmaps or lists track available blocks. Updates spanning allocation, data and metadata need crash consistency, often via journaling or copy-on-write techniques. File permissions control access independently of block placement.

sections.title: Data reachability, metadata and disk movement
sections.body: An indirect block contains addresses, not user payload. If a block contains p addresses, one single-indirect pointer reaches p data blocks, a double-indirect pointer reaches up to p², and a triple-indirect pointer up to p³. Add direct blocks, then multiply reachable data blocks by data-block size. Metadata space and metadata I/O are separate counts: following a double-indirect pointer may read two index blocks before the data block unless cached. Linked allocation makes sequential access natural but locating an arbitrary logical block requires link traversal. Contiguous allocation permits arithmetic location but constrains growth and can suffer external fragmentation. Disk scheduling calculations apply to a moving-head model: add absolute differences of consecutive head positions and follow the specified direction/end/wrap rules.

examples.prompt: Capacity with 10 direct pointers plus one indirect pointer

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Use 1024-byte blocks and 4-byte addresses, so indirect capacity=\(1024/4=256\) addresses. An indirect block’s entries are four-byte addresses; dividing block bytes by pointer bytes gives 256 data pointers.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Total reachable data blocks=10+256=266. The ten direct blocks are additional to the indirect block’s 256 target blocks.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Maximum data capacity under this simplified structure=\(266\cdot1024=272384\) bytes, excluding metadata itself. File data capacity counts user-data blocks; the index block consumes storage but is not another user-data block.

examples.strategy: Count reachable data blocks separately from the indirect metadata block.
examples.answer: Maximum data capacity under this simplified structure=\(266\cdot1024=272384\) bytes, excluding metadata itself.
examples.verification: \(266\cdot1024=272384\) bytes. Allocating every reachable data block also requires the separate indirect metadata block.

steps: To reach logical block 4, start at logical block 0.
Follow four next-block links unless a separate cached index supplies the location.
Contiguous allocation computes its address directly; the representation changes cost.

pitfalls: An indirect block is metadata, not an additional file-data block.
Count cached and uncached metadata according to the question.
revision: Pointers per index block=block bytes/pointer bytes.
Directories map names; allocation maps logical data to blocks.

checks.hint: Divide bytes by pointer size.

checks.hint: Multiply block count by size.

name: Databases
description: Model, query and protect your data

lessons.title: ER modelling, relational schemas and integrity
lessons.intuition: A database model captures which facts exist and how they relate. ER diagrams express entities and relationships at a conceptual level; relational schemas encode them as tables with keys and constraints that prevent invalid states.

sections.title: ER concepts and mapping
sections.body: Entities have identifying attributes; relationships link entities with cardinality and participation constraints. A one-to-many relationship is often represented by a foreign key on the many side. A many-to-many relationship becomes its own relation with foreign keys to both sides and any relationship attributes. Weak entities require an owner key plus their partial identifier.

sections.title: Relational keys
sections.body: A superkey uniquely determines a tuple; a candidate key is a minimal superkey. Choose one candidate as primary key. Keys can span multiple attributes, and additional unique constraints can express alternate keys. Relations in the mathematical model are sets of tuples, unlike SQL’s default duplicate-preserving query results.

sections.title: Integrity
sections.body: Domain constraints restrict value types/ranges; entity integrity requires primary-key values not be NULL; referential integrity requires a non-NULL foreign key to match an allowed referenced key. Deleting a referenced tuple may be rejected or trigger defined cascading/set-null actions. A foreign key need not be unique on the referencing side.

sections.title: Keys express constraints rather than sample coincidences
sections.body: A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies every possible legal row under the schema constraints. Seeing distinct names in one sample table does not prove name is a key. A superkey may contain unnecessary attributes; a primary key is one chosen candidate key. A relationship can need its own attributes: a grade belongs to a student’s enrollment in a course, rather than to the student or course alone. For repeated enrollments, the student/course pair ceases to identify each event and a term or attempt identifier is needed. Weak entities depend on an owner plus their partial key. Foreign-key constraints enforce that referenced rows exist, but cardinality, nullability and total participation can need additional uniqueness or application/database constraints.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Student has key student_id; Course has key course_id. Entity identifiers are inherited into the relationship to state which student and which course participate.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Because many students take many courses, create Enrollment(student_id,course_id,grade). Neither a student nor a course alone identifies an enrollment, because each can participate many times.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The pair can be its key if each student takes each course once, and both identifiers are foreign keys. Repeated offerings would need an additional term/attempt attribute. The pair is minimal only under the one-enrollment-per-student/course assumption; adding repeated terms changes that constraint.

examples.strategy: Represent the many-to-many relationship explicitly and derive its key from event uniqueness.
examples.answer: The pair can be its key if each student takes each course once, and both identifiers are foreign keys. Repeated offerings would need an additional term/attempt attribute.
examples.verification: One student in two courses and two students in one course produce distinct pairs without duplicating entity details or losing relationship grades.

steps: If student_id alone identifies a row, {student_id,name} also identifies it.
The larger set is a superkey.
It is not a candidate key because removing name still preserves uniqueness.

pitfalls: A candidate key is minimal by inclusion, not simply smallest-looking.
A foreign key is not necessarily a unique identifier.

lessons.title: Relational algebra, tuple calculus and SQL
lessons.intuition: A query describes a derived relation. Algebra describes operations to produce it, while calculus describes a logical condition on desired tuples. SQL uses related ideas but adds practical semantics for duplicates, NULL and grouping.

sections.title: Algebra and calculus
sections.body: Selection σ filters tuples; projection π keeps named columns and removes duplicates in set-based algebra. Cartesian product pairs every tuple; a join filters combinations by a condition. Union and difference require compatible schemas. Tuple relational calculus uses predicates on tuples; safe/range-restricted expressions ensure finite, domain-independent results.

sections.title: SQL order and joins
sections.body: Conceptually FROM/JOIN establishes sources, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT chooses expressions, and ORDER BY orders results. An inner join requires a match; an outer join also retains unmatched rows with NULL-filled columns. Filtering an outer-joined table in WHERE can discard the unmatched rows and change the intended semantics.

sections.title: Duplicates, aggregates and NULL
sections.body: SELECT ordinarily keeps duplicates; DISTINCT removes them. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. SUM/AVG ordinarily ignore NULL inputs. Comparisons involving NULL usually yield UNKNOWN; WHERE retains only TRUE. Use IS NULL rather than =NULL. SQL OR/AND follows three-valued logic in such cases.

sections.title: Trace bags, nulls and grouping explicitly
sections.body: Under SQL bag semantics, a join can multiply duplicates: if a key has two matching left rows and three matching right rows, their equality join contributes six rows. DISTINCT removes duplicates at its specified stage and cannot be assumed throughout. WHERE evaluates predicates on source rows, then GROUP BY partitions survivors and HAVING filters completed groups. Null comparisons normally yield UNKNOWN, so NULL=NULL does not become TRUE; use IS NULL to test nullness. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) and AVG(column) ignore nulls. For an empty input without grouping, COUNT returns zero while many other aggregates return NULL. NOT IN can be poisoned by a null comparison; reasoning through the three-valued truth conditions is safer than blindly rewriting it as an anti-join.

examples.prompt: Count students per department with at least three students

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Group Student rows by dept. Rows with the same department value contribute to the same aggregate group.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Use SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Student GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*)>=3. COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group and HAVING applies the threshold to that computed group result.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The group filter belongs in HAVING; WHERE cannot directly filter by the completed aggregate count. A row-level WHERE condition cannot use the aggregate count of a group that has not yet been formed.

examples.strategy: Form groups before evaluating a predicate over their aggregate count.
examples.answer: The group filter belongs in HAVING; WHERE cannot directly filter by the completed aggregate count.
examples.verification: A department with two rows is absent, one with three rows appears with count 3; SELECT and GROUP BY use the same grouping attribute.

steps: There are three rows, so COUNT(*)=3.
Only two have non-NULL column values, so COUNT(value)=2.

pitfalls: Projection in relational algebra eliminates duplicates; SQL SELECT does not by default.
NULL is not an ordinary comparable value.
revision: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

checks.prompt: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregation?
checks.hint: Group predicates require already formed groups.
checks.explanation: HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters source rows before aggregation.

checks.prompt: Relations with 3 and 4 tuples have how many tuples in their Cartesian product?
checks.hint: Every tuple pairs with every tuple.
checks.explanation: 3×4=12 pairs.

lessons.concept: A query describes a derived relation. Algebra describes operations to produce it, while calculus describes a logical condition on desired tuples. SQL uses related ideas but adds practical semantics for duplicates, NULL and grouping.
lessons.method: Selection σ filters tuples; projection π keeps named columns and removes duplicates in set-based algebra. Cartesian product pairs every tuple; a join filters combinations by a condition. Union and difference require compatible schemas. Tuple relational calculus uses predicates on tuples; safe/range-restricted expressions ensure finite, domain-independent results. Conceptually FROM/JOIN establishes sources, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT chooses expressions, and ORDER BY orders results. An inner join requires a match; an outer join also retains unmatched rows with NULL-filled columns. Filtering an outer-joined table in WHERE can discard the unmatched rows and change the intended semantics. SELECT ordinarily keeps duplicates; DISTINCT removes them. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. SUM/AVG ordinarily ignore NULL inputs. Comparisons involving NULL usually yield UNKNOWN; WHERE retains only TRUE. Use IS NULL rather than =NULL. SQL OR/AND follows three-valued logic in such cases. Under SQL bag semantics, a join can multiply duplicates: if a key has two matching left rows and three matching right rows, their equality join contributes six rows. DISTINCT removes duplicates at its specified stage and cannot be assumed throughout. WHERE evaluates predicates on source rows, then GROUP BY partitions survivors and HAVING filters completed groups. Null comparisons normally yield UNKNOWN, so NULL=NULL does not become TRUE; use IS NULL to test nullness. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) and AVG(column) ignore nulls. For an empty input without grouping, COUNT returns zero while many other aggregates return NULL. NOT IN can be poisoned by a null comparison; reasoning through the three-valued truth conditions is safer than blindly rewriting it as an anti-join.
lessons.example: Count students per department with at least three students

gateGuide.recognize: SQL uses bags by default and three-valued logic for nulls. Relational algebra commonly uses sets; keep the semantics explicit.
method: Trace FROM/join rows, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and projection; apply DISTINCT only if requested.
For null comparisons use TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN; WHERE retains TRUE rows.
For nested queries identify correlated variables and test empty inputs, duplicates and nulls.

traps.claim: COUNT(column) counts every row
traps.why: It excludes nulls in that column; COUNT(*) counts rows.

traps.claim: NOT IN is always interchangeable with NOT EXISTS
traps.why: A null in the subquery can make NOT IN UNKNOWN, while a suitable NOT EXISTS correlation behaves differently.

formulas.meaning: Select qualifying rows, then project attributes A, under relational-algebra set semantics.
Theta join; SQL duplicate counts can differ from set algebra.

lessons.title: Functional dependencies and normal forms
lessons.intuition: Normalization controls redundancy caused by dependencies. A dependency is a rule about every valid database state, not a coincidence in one sample table. Begin by computing keys; normal-form tests depend on superkeys and prime attributes.

sections.title: Closure and inference
sections.body: \(X\to Y\) says equal values on X force equal values on Y. Attribute closure X⁺ starts with X and repeatedly adds RHS attributes whose LHS is already present. If X⁺ contains the whole schema, X is a superkey; remove redundant attributes to test minimality. Armstrong’s reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity support sound dependency inference.

sections.title: 2NF, 3NF and BCNF
sections.body: After atomic-value 1NF, 2NF rules out dependence of a nonprime attribute on a proper subset of a candidate key. In 3NF, every nontrivial X→A has X a superkey or A prime, meaning in some candidate key. BCNF drops the prime-attribute exception and requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. BCNF implies 3NF, but not conversely.

sections.title: Decomposition
sections.body: Lossless join means decomposed relations reconstruct exactly the original valid relation, with no spurious tuples. For a binary decomposition into R1,R2, their intersection determining all of R1 or all of R2 under F⁺ is the usual lossless criterion. Dependency preservation permits checking original dependencies without joining. These are separate properties; a BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation.

sections.title: Closure, decomposition and independent guarantees
sections.body: Attribute closure is an inference procedure: start with X, apply any FD whose entire left side is present, add its right side, and repeat to a fixed point. A key needs closure equal to all relation attributes and minimality under attribute removal. BCNF restricts every nontrivial determinant to a superkey; 3NF additionally permits a prime right-hand attribute. Lossless decomposition means every legal original relation is exactly reconstructed by joining its projections. It does not merely mean that tables share a column. Dependency preservation means constraints can be enforced within component relations without joining them. Projection includes all implied dependencies on each component, not just original FDs with visibly matching columns. A decomposition can satisfy one guarantee and fail the other, so state separate proofs.

examples.prompt: Normalize R(A,B,C) with \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\)

steps.title: Find a minimal key
steps.explanation: A determines B, then B determines C. No dependency can introduce A, so every key must contain A; A alone is the sole candidate key.

steps.title: Test the violating dependency
steps.explanation: B is not a superkey, and C is nonprime because the only candidate key is A. The nontrivial \(B\to C\) fails both BCNF and 3NF.

steps.title: Decompose and prove losslessness
steps.explanation: The shared attribute determines all of R₂, satisfying the binary lossless-join criterion. A mere shared attribute would not be sufficient.
steps.equation: R_1=AB,\quad R_2=BC,\quad R_1\cap R_2=\{B\},\quad B\to BC

steps.title: Verify preservation and resulting normal forms
steps.explanation: Each original dependency can be checked locally. A and B respectively are keys of their new relations, so both relations are in BCNF.
steps.equation: A\to B\text{ in }AB,\qquad B\to C\text{ in }BC

examples.given: R(A,B,C), with FDs \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\) and their logical consequences.
examples.goal: Find a key, violations and a lossless dependency-preserving decomposition.
examples.strategy: Compute closures before testing normal forms; verify decomposition properties independently.
examples.answer: AB and BC form a lossless, dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition.
examples.verification: Join projections of any relation satisfying the FDs: a B value can have only one C, preventing spurious alternative C values for an A.

examples.prompt: Compute closure with \(A\to B\), \(BC\to D\) and \(A\to C\)
steps: Add B and C from the two A dependencies.
Now BC is present, so add D. \(A^+=\{A,B,C,D\}\).

pitfalls: Sample rows do not prove a dependency holds universally.
Lossless and dependency-preserving are different tests.
revision: BCNF: every nontrivial determinant is a superkey.

checks.prompt: What is the BCNF rule for a nontrivial functional dependency \(X\to Y\)?
checks.hint: BCNF removes the prime-RHS exception from 3NF.
checks.explanation: Every nontrivial determinant must be a superkey. A prime RHS can permit 3NF but does not by itself satisfy BCNF.
options: Y must be the primary key
X must be a single attribute

checks.prompt: How many attributes are in B⁺ for the same dependencies?
checks.hint: A cannot be inferred from B.

method: Compute attribute closure using all applicable functional dependencies until no attribute changes.
Find minimal keys; identify prime attributes, then test each relevant dependency against 3NF/BCNF definitions.
For a binary split test the intersection dependency for losslessness; for preservation check dependencies inferable within projected schemas.

traps.claim: BCNF guarantees dependency preservation
traps.why: BCNF decomposition may lose an FD that then requires a join to enforce.

traps.claim: A lossless join means no duplicated rows at all
traps.why: It means joining projections reconstructs exactly the original valid relation, without spurious tuples.

formulas.meaning: Test all implied dependencies, not merely the listed ones.

lessons.title: File organization and B/B+ tree indexing
lessons.intuition: An index is an auxiliary route to data, not the data model itself. On-disk indexes use high branching factors to reduce expensive page reads. Equality and range queries can prefer different organizations.

sections.title: File layout
sections.body: Heap files place records in convenient free space and favour insertion without key order. Sorted files favour ordered scans but make insertion maintenance costly. Hash organization targets equality buckets and generally does not preserve ordering. A clustered organization aligns data placement with index order; a secondary index may require scattered data-page fetches.

sections.title: B-tree family
sections.body: B and B+ trees remain balanced and store many separator keys per page. In a common B+ design, internal nodes guide search while data entries are at leaves, which are linked for range scans. Definitions of “order” vary: read whether it means maximum children, maximum keys or minimum occupancy. Splits, redistribution and merges preserve occupancy and balance.

sections.title: Cost reasoning
sections.body: With fanout f and many entries, height grows roughly logarithmically in f. Point search follows one root-to-leaf path; a range search locates its starting leaf then walks linked leaves. Dense indexes have an entry for every relevant key/record convention; sparse indexes have selected entries and ordinarily require ordered data. Include data-page reads separately when an index does not contain the required record.

sections.title: Derive capacity from page layout
sections.body: An internal B+ tree page with f children normally needs f pointers and f−1 separator keys; a leaf page instead needs key/record entries and a next-leaf pointer, potentially with other metadata. Subtract reserved bytes before deriving each capacity. Maximum fanout is not minimum occupancy: split rules and root exceptions affect minimum and maximum tree heights. Search chooses an internal pointer using separators until a leaf, then checks the actual key. A range query locates its first leaf once and follows leaf links, but fetching records through an unclustered index can add scattered data-page I/O. A clustered layout tends to group nearby key values in nearby data pages. Counting tree levels alone estimates index traversal, not necessarily the entire query’s disk cost.

examples.prompt: Estimate maximum leaves for a B+ tree with 3 levels and fanout 4

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The root is level 1 and can point to 4 internal nodes. Level numbering starts at the root as level 1; three levels therefore contain two pointer expansions.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Each internal node can point to 4 leaves. Each of the four internal nodes can supply four independent leaf children under the maximum-fanout assumption.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Maximum leaves=4×4=16, excluding leaf entry capacity from this count. This is the maximum number of leaf pages, not the maximum records. Record capacity additionally requires entries per leaf.

examples.strategy: Count child pointers per level and keep leaf entry capacity out of leaf-node count.
examples.answer: Maximum leaves=4×4=16, excluding leaf entry capacity from this count.
examples.verification: Level counts are 1,4,16. Multiplying by four a third time would erroneously count an extra level.

examples.prompt: Range query using a B+ index
steps: Search down to the leaf containing the first key at least the lower bound.
Scan that leaf and follow next-leaf links.
Stop once the upper bound is exceeded; do not restart root search for each successive key.

pitfalls: B-tree “order” conventions are not universal.
An index-only search differs from an index lookup plus record fetch.
revision: B+ leaf links support range scans; hashing favours equality.

checks.prompt: A root with fanout 5 points directly to leaves. What is the maximum number of leaves?
checks.hint: One child pointer selects one leaf.
checks.explanation: At most 5 leaves.

checks.prompt: A disk page of 4096 bytes stores fixed-size 128-byte records without overhead. How many fit?
checks.hint: Divide page bytes by record bytes.

Trace lookup, split and redistribution using the specified occupancy convention.
For cost count page reads, consider root caching and distinguish clustered range scans from repeated unclustered record fetches.

traps.claim: B+ tree internal keys store every record
traps.why: Records or record pointers are normally at leaves; internal keys guide traversal.

traps.claim: An index makes every range query cheap
traps.why: An unclustered range can require many scattered data-page reads, especially when many rows qualify.

formulas.meaning: Internal fanout f with pointer size p, separator size k and available bytes B.

lessons.title: Transactions, serializability and concurrency control
lessons.intuition: Transactions group operations into a unit whose intermediate effects must be controlled. Concurrency can improve throughput, but interleavings must preserve an allowed relationship to serial execution and support recovery when work fails.

sections.title: ACID and anomalies
sections.body: Atomicity gives all-or-nothing effects; consistency preserves declared invariants when transactions themselves are correct; isolation controls interference; durability preserves committed effects after recovery. Lost updates overwrite another transaction’s changes. Dirty reads observe uncommitted writes. Nonrepeatable reads and phantoms involve changing rows or predicate result sets across reads.

sections.title: Conflict serializability
sections.body: Two operations conflict if they are in different transactions, access the same item, and at least one writes. Add Ti→Tj when Ti’s conflicting operation precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable iff this precedence graph is acyclic; a topological order gives an equivalent serial ordering. Read-read pairs create no edge. Conflict serializability is stronger than some other semantic notions of serializability.

sections.title: Locks and recovery
sections.body: Two-phase locking first acquires locks, then releases without acquiring new ones. It guarantees conflict serializability under the standard model but can deadlock. Strict variants retain required exclusive locks until commit/abort to prevent cascading effects. Write-ahead logging requires appropriate log records be durable before related dirty data pages are written. Recovery may redo committed work and undo uncommitted work according to its logging scheme.

sections.title: Three graphs of reasoning: conflict, reads and locks
sections.body: Conflict ordering constrains transactions when actions from different transactions touch the same item and at least one is a write. Read/read order adds no conflict edge. A directed cycle prevents any serial order satisfying all conflict constraints. Recovery instead follows which write supplied each read: committing a reader before that writer risks a committed dependency on an aborted value. Cascadeless schedules prevent reading uncommitted writes; strict schedules also prevent overwriting uncommitted writes. Two-phase locking forbids new lock acquisitions after the first release and guarantees conflict serializability, but can deadlock. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until completion, preventing dirty reads/writes of protected items; terminology for holding all locks is often called rigorous 2PL. Distinguish protocol rules from properties inferred for one particular schedule.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: W1(X) before R2(X) adds \(T_1\to T_2\). A write followed by another transaction’s read conflicts, so any equivalent serial order must place T1 before T2.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: W2(Y) before R1(Y) adds \(T_2\to T_1\). The conflict on Y imposes the opposite ordering, T2 before T1.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The graph has a cycle, so the schedule is not conflict serializable. No serial transaction order can satisfy both directions; the two-edge cycle is a certificate of conflict nonserializability.

examples.strategy: Build precedence edges only for same-item conflicts across different transactions.
examples.answer: The graph has a cycle, so the schedule is not conflict serializable.
examples.verification: Try serial T1,T2 and T2,T1: the former violates the Y constraint, the latter violates the X constraint. Commit/recovery properties are separate.

steps: The reads of X do not conflict.
W1(Y) before R2(Y) creates only \(T_1\to T_2\).
The graph is acyclic; serial order T1,T2 is conflict-equivalent.

pitfalls: Read-read overlap does not create a conflict.
Two-phase locking can still deadlock.
revision: WAL orders logging before corresponding data writes.

checks.prompt: Which pair creates a conflict between distinct transactions on the same item?
checks.hint: Conflict requires different transactions, same item and a write.
checks.explanation: Read/write, write/read and write/write pairs conflict. Read/read does not.
options: A pair containing at least one write
Every pair even on different items
Only writes in the same transaction

checks.prompt: A precedence graph contains \(T_1\to T_2\) and \(T_2\to T_1\). How many vertices are in this directed cycle?
checks.hint: Follow the two opposite edges.
checks.explanation: The cycle involves the two transactions.

traps.claim: Every serializable schedule is recoverable
traps.why: T2 can read T1’s write and commit before T1 aborts even if the conflict order is serializable.

traps.claim: Every cycle proves lack of view serializability
traps.why: It disproves conflict serializability; blind writes can permit view-serializable schedules outside that class.

formulas.meaning: An earlier conflicting action of Ti precedes an action of Tj on the same item; at least one is a write.
Recoverability requires writer Ti to commit before reader Tj commits when Tj reads Ti’s value.

lessons.title: Layering, switching and network performance
lessons.intuition: A network separates services into layers so each solves a manageable part of delivery. Packets share infrastructure, while circuits reserve capacity. Delay depends on several physical and queueing effects, so bandwidth and latency are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Layers and encapsulation
sections.body: An application message becomes transport data, then a network packet, then a link frame under common Internet layering. Each layer adds addressing/control information appropriate to its scope. A router forwards network-layer packets; a typical Ethernet switch forwards link-layer frames. End-to-end services and per-link services solve different problems.

sections.title: Switching models
sections.body: Circuit switching reserves a route or channel allocation, potentially with setup overhead and unused reserved capacity. Packet switching shares links among packets and can queue under load. Datagram packets can be routed independently; a virtual circuit establishes logical forwarding state before transfer, typically using a label on subsequent packets. A logical virtual circuit is not necessarily a physically reserved circuit.

sections.title: Delay and throughput
sections.body: Transmission delay=L/R for L bits on rate R; propagation delay=distance/signal speed. Processing and queueing add further delay. Store-and-forward requires a full packet before forwarding in the basic model. Bottleneck link rate constrains sustained throughput. With multiple packets and links, serialization can be pipelined; don’t multiply entire end-to-end latency by packet count automatically.

sections.title: Serialization, propagation and pipeline overlap
sections.body: A link serializes a packet by placing its bits onto the medium over L/R seconds. Once a bit is launched, propagation carries it across the link over distance/speed seconds. Doubling packet length doubles serialization but does not change an individual bit’s propagation delay. A store-and-forward router must receive the complete packet before starting its outgoing serialization. Across equal-rate links, successive packets can overlap on different links; the first packet pays the full path serialization, while later packets emerge at the bottleneck packet interval under the simplified no-queuing model. Routers replace link-layer framing for the next hop while forwarding toward the network-layer destination. Circuit setup and reserved capacity belong to a different service model than ordinary statistical multiplexing.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Convert to bits: \(1500\cdot8=12000\). The rate is given in bits per second, so leaving packet size in bytes would undercount time by a factor of eight.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Transmission delay=\(\frac{12000}{12\cdot10^6}=0.001\) s. Mbps uses decimal millions here; the resulting quotient is in seconds.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: That is 1 ms, excluding propagation and queueing. This calculation concerns serialization only. Distance or router delays cannot be inferred from packet size and link rate alone.

examples.strategy: Convert packet bytes to bits, then divide by bit rate.
examples.answer: That is 1 ms, excluding propagation and queueing.
examples.verification: 12,000 bits at 12,000,000 bits/s is 1/1000 s=1 ms, with consistent dimensions.

examples.prompt: Two store-and-forward links at the same rate, no other delay
steps: The first packet needs one transmission time on each link, total 2t.
For N packets, after the first link finishes one it can send the next while the next link forwards the previous.
Completion is (N+1)t for two equal links under these assumptions, not 2Nt.

pitfalls: Convert bytes to bits before dividing by bit rate.
Faster bandwidth does not reduce propagation distance.

checks.prompt: A 1000-byte packet uses an 8 Mbps link. What is transmission delay in milliseconds?
checks.hint: Convert bytes to bits.

checks.prompt: Propagation distance is 600 km and speed 200000 km/s. What is propagation delay in milliseconds?
checks.hint: Divide distance by speed and convert seconds.

method: Identify each layer’s addressing and service, then trace encapsulation across routers.
Separate serialization from propagation, queuing and processing.

traps.why: It depends on distance and propagation speed; serialization depends on packet length and link rate.

traps.claim: Every layer uses the same destination address
traps.why: Link destination is normally the next hop; network destination usually remains the remote host.

formulas.meaning: L bits at R bits/s.
Distance d and signal speed s in consistent units.
Sum over modeled hops; queuing must be supplied or modeled.

lessons.title: Error detection, MAC and Ethernet
lessons.prerequisite: Binary polynomials, frames and shared media.
lessons.intuition: The link layer moves frames over one link and manages its local addressing and error checks. Error detection identifies some corrupt frames; it is not automatically error correction. Shared-medium access rules matter only where senders actually contend for the same medium.

sections.title: Parity, checksums and CRC
sections.body: A parity bit detects any odd number of bit flips but can miss an even number. Internet-style checksums use one’s-complement arithmetic. CRC treats bits as polynomial coefficients over GF(2): addition/subtraction is XOR. Append r zeros for a degree-r generator, divide, and append the r-bit remainder. A receiver divides the received codeword; a nonzero remainder detects an error.

sections.title: Medium access
sections.body: ALOHA transmits with probabilistic contention; carrier-sense protocols listen before transmitting. Classic half-duplex Ethernet uses CSMA/CD, detecting collisions and backing off. The minimum frame time must support collision detection over the collision domain under its physical assumptions. Full-duplex switched Ethernet has separate bidirectional links and does not use collision detection.

sections.title: Ethernet switching
sections.body: MAC addresses identify local link interfaces. A learning switch records the source MAC and ingress port. Known destination addresses are forwarded to the corresponding port; unknown destinations and relevant broadcasts are flooded according to VLAN/topology rules. Routers separate network-layer domains; a link switch does not usually choose routes by IP prefix.

sections.title: Why sequence-space bounds prevent ambiguity
sections.body: A sender may have multiple frames outstanding while acknowledgments are delayed. Sequence numbers wrap, so a delayed old frame must not be mistaken for a new frame with the same number. Selective repeat accepts and buffers a window of out-of-order frames; disjoint old and new windows require the usual half-sequence-space bound. Go-back-N’s receiver ordinarily accepts only the next expected frame, yielding a different maximum sender window. State those receiver models before using memorized bounds. CRC treats bitstrings as polynomials over GF(2), so subtraction is XOR without borrow. Appending r zeros multiplies data by xʳ; the division remainder produces a codeword divisible by the generator. Detection guarantees depend on the error polynomial and generator, not just the remainder’s length.

examples.prompt: Detect a single flipped bit with even parity

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Suppose data has an even number of 1s and parity bit 0. The sender chooses the parity bit so the complete protected word has an even number of ones.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: One flipped bit changes overall parity to odd. One bit flip changes the number of ones by plus or minus one, which reverses its parity.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The receiver detects mismatch, but cannot locate the bad bit from parity alone. Mismatch reports inconsistency but does not identify which of the possible bit positions changed.

examples.strategy: Evaluate parity detection separately from correction capability.
examples.answer: The receiver detects mismatch, but cannot locate the bad bit from parity alone.
examples.verification: Two flipped bits can restore even parity and escape detection; the result is a single-bit detection guarantee, not an arbitrary-error guarantee.

steps: Generator degree is 3, so divide appended data 1001000 by 1011 using XOR.
First XOR gives 0010000; align again and XOR to get 0000110.
Remainder is 110; transmit 1001110. Dividing this codeword by 1011 gives zero remainder.

pitfalls: CRC division uses XOR without carries.
Modern full-duplex Ethernet does not use CSMA/CD.
revision: Degree-r CRC appends r check bits.
Switch learns source MAC, forwards by destination MAC.

checks.prompt: Which statement about modern full-duplex switched Ethernet is correct?
checks.hint: Separate full-duplex links from a shared half-duplex collision domain.
checks.explanation: Full-duplex switched Ethernet does not use CSMA/CD; classic half-duplex shared-medium Ethernet does.
options: It uses CSMA/CD on every link
It does not use collision detection in the classic shared-medium sense
It routes by longest IP prefix at every basic switch

checks.prompt: An even-parity codeword suffers exactly one bit flip. What is the number of parity violations detected?
checks.hint: One flip changes parity.
checks.explanation: The single parity check fails once; it detects but does not locate the error.

lessons.title: Distance-vector and link-state routing
lessons.prerequisite: Graphs, shortest paths and link costs.
lessons.intuition: Routers need a distributed way to learn where to send packets. Distance-vector exchanges route estimates with neighbours; link-state distributes topology so each router can compute routes locally. The information each approach shares explains its failure modes.

sections.title: Distance-vector update
sections.body: A router x estimates Dx(y)=minᵥ[c(x,v)+Dv(y)] over neighbours v. Each advertisement supplies a neighbour’s current estimate. Updates may be asynchronous and transient inconsistencies arise when links fail. A destination that becomes unreachable may have increasing estimates passed around, producing count-to-infinity.

sections.title: Mitigations and link-state
sections.body: Split horizon avoids advertising a route back on the interface from which it was learned; poisoned reverse explicitly advertises an infinite metric in that direction. These do not solve every possible loop topology. Link-state routers discover neighbours/costs, flood sequenced link-state advertisements and run Dijkstra on their assembled topology. Sequence numbers and aging prevent stale information from circulating indefinitely.

sections.title: Forwarding versus routing
sections.body: Routing computes and updates the control-plane table; forwarding uses it for individual packets. A next hop need not be the destination itself. Correct convergence is distinct from instantaneous consistency during updates. Compare control traffic, stored knowledge and recovery behaviour rather than assuming one protocol is universally superior.

sections.title: Local advertisements versus global topology
sections.body: A distance-vector router stores estimates learned from neighbors and chooses the neighbor minimizing link cost plus advertised remaining distance. If a neighbor’s route actually depends on the router itself, stale messages after a failure can create a loop. Split horizon and poison reverse suppress some immediate feedback, but are not universal proofs against every multi-router convergence problem. Link-state routers flood link information so each can compute from a topology snapshot; inconsistent or old snapshots can still produce transient behavior. After routes are installed, forwarding chooses among destination prefixes by longest match. A more specific route overrides a broader matching route even if the broader one appears first or has a lower cost metric; route selection within a prefix and forwarding specificity are separate stages.

examples.prompt: Update destination D using two neighbours

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Neighbour A costs 2 and advertises distance 5; candidate cost is 7. The advertisement excludes the cost of reaching the neighbor, so that local cost must be included.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Neighbour B costs 4 and advertises distance 1; candidate cost is 5. A more expensive first hop can still have a cheaper end-to-end route because its advertised suffix is shorter.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Choose B with total 5. The direct link price alone did not determine the best route. The decision compares complete candidate route totals, not individual links in isolation.

examples.strategy: Add each local link cost to that neighbor’s advertised remaining distance.
examples.answer: Choose B with total 5. The direct link price alone did not determine the best route.
examples.verification: Via A costs 2+5=7; via B costs 4+1=5. Choosing B minimizes the advertised total under this snapshot.

examples.prompt: Understand a stale estimate after failure
steps: A previously reaches D directly, while B’s route to D uses A.
After A loses the destination link, B may still advertise its old route through A.
If A trusts that advertisement, A and B can route toward each other while increasing metrics; stale dependencies create the loop.

pitfalls: Distance-vector advertisements are distances, not full topology maps in the basic model.
Split horizon is not a universal cure for every multi-router loop.
revision: Link-state computes shortest paths from flooded topology.

checks.prompt: Link to a neighbour costs 3 and its advertised destination distance is 7. What candidate total is offered?
checks.hint: Add local and advertised costs.

checks.prompt: Candidates are 8,12 and 6. What destination metric is selected?
checks.hint: Take the smallest feasible candidate.

gateGuide.recognize: Distance-vector and link-state protocols maintain different knowledge. Forwarding uses a routing table; routing computes it.
method: For distance-vector update each destination via every neighbor using that neighbor’s advertised distance.
For link state assemble the topology and run a shortest-path calculation.

traps.claim: Distance-vector updates use the neighbor’s route as instant global truth
traps.why: Stale advertisements can cause loops and count-to-infinity after failures.

traps.claim: The first matching route always wins
traps.why: Forwarding normally chooses the longest matching prefix, independent of table listing order.

lessons.title: IPv4, CIDR and network address translation
lessons.intuition: An IPv4 address contains 32 bits. CIDR says how many leading bits define the routing prefix. NAT rewrites selected addresses and ports, often allowing several private hosts to share a public address, but it changes end-to-end addressing assumptions.

sections.title: CIDR arithmetic
sections.body: A /p prefix leaves 32−p varying bits and contains 2^(32−p) total addresses. In conventional multiaccess subnets, network and broadcast addresses are not assignable hosts, giving two fewer; /31 point-to-point and /32 cases require different treatment. Masking an address with the subnet mask gives its network prefix. Block boundaries follow the mask, not arbitrary decimal rounding.

sections.title: Longest-prefix match
sections.body: A packet destination may match several routes. Select the matching route with the largest prefix length, because it identifies the most specific region. The default /0 matches everything but loses to any more-specific match. A route’s prefix need not match a classful address boundary; CIDR replaced that restriction.

sections.title: NAT/PAT
sections.body: Address translation rewrites private/public addresses; port translation distinguishes multiple internal transport sessions sharing an external IP. The device keeps mappings and updates required checksums. Incoming connections need a mapping or explicit forwarding arrangement. NAT is not equivalent to a complete security policy and can complicate protocols embedding addresses in payloads.

sections.title: Bits determine alignment and aggregation
sections.body: A /p prefix fixes the first p address bits and leaves 32−p host bits. The network address sets those remaining bits to zero; under ordinary subnet semantics the directed broadcast sets them all to one. A /26 leaves six bits, so last-octet boundaries occur at multiples of 64. Aggregating two /p blocks into /p−1 is valid only if their prefixes differ in the last prefix bit and share all earlier bits. Numerically adjacent blocks can cross an alignment boundary and fail this test. Conventional host-count subtraction reserves network and broadcast addresses, but /31 point-to-point addressing and /32 host routes use different conventions. Private addressing, NAT and CIDR solve different needs: a private address is not itself a routing prefix-length rule.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: There are 6 host bits, so blocks contain 64 addresses. Prefix length 26 leaves 32−26=6 host bits, giving 64 total addresses per block.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: The last-octet ranges begin 0,64,128,192; 70 lies in 64–127. Integer division of the final octet by 64 identifies its block: floor(70/64)=1, beginning at 64.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Network is 192.168.1.64, conventional broadcast .127, with hosts .65–.126. Under conventional subnet semantics the first and last addresses are network and broadcast; they are excluded from the host range.

examples.strategy: Find the aligned CIDR block by host-bit width and boundary multiples.
examples.answer: Network is 192.168.1.64, conventional broadcast .127, with hosts .65–.126.
examples.verification: 70 AND 192 gives 64 in the last octet. The host range contains 62 addresses, from 65 through 126 inclusive.

steps: All three cover the destination in this example.
The /24 route has the longest prefix.
Forward using its next hop; the fact that /16 covers more addresses does not give it priority.

pitfalls: Total addresses and assignable hosts are different counts.
Do not subtract two blindly for /31 or /32.
revision: Choose the longest matching route prefix.

checks.prompt: How many total IPv4 addresses are in a /27 prefix?
checks.hint: There are 5 host bits.
checks.explanation: 2⁵=32 addresses.

checks.prompt: How many conventionally assignable host addresses are in a /26 multiaccess subnet?
checks.hint: Subtract network and broadcast from the total.
checks.explanation: 64−2=62 hosts under the stated convention.

lessons.title: IPv4 fragmentation step by step
lessons.prerequisite: IPv4 headers, byte counts and division.
lessons.intuition: An IP datagram may exceed a link’s maximum transmission unit. Fragmentation divides its payload while preserving enough information to reassemble at the destination. Headers are repeated for every fragment, and offsets locate payload bytes rather than whole datagram bytes.

sections.title: Payload capacity
sections.body: MTU limits the total IP fragment length including its own IP header. With header H, payload capacity is MTU−H. Every nonfinal fragment payload must be a multiple of 8 bytes, so use floor((MTU−H)/8)×8 when creating maximal nonfinal fragments. The final payload may be smaller and need not be an eight-byte multiple.

sections.title: Header interpretation
sections.body: Fragments share the relevant source,destination,protocol and identification association. The fragment offset measures where this payload starts in the original payload, in units of 8 bytes. MF=1 says more fragments follow; MF=0 identifies the final portion, not necessarily a complete unfragmented original. DF forbids fragmentation, so an oversize packet must be handled by failure/feedback under the protocol instead.

sections.title: Reassembly reasoning
sections.body: Add payload lengths to verify the original payload total. Calculate offsets cumulatively from payload, excluding repeated headers. IPv4 permits routers to fragment when allowed; destination reassembly handles the pieces. Loss of one needed fragment prevents normal complete delivery of the original datagram, adding a reason large fragmented packets can be fragile.

sections.title: Offsets describe the original payload
sections.body: Each fragment is a separate IP packet with its own header and total length. The offset identifies where its data belongs in the original IP payload; counting previous fragment headers would misplace reassembly. Nonfinal payload sizes must be multiples of eight because the next offset has eight-byte granularity. The last payload may have a remainder. Fragmentation adds header overhead, so summed transmitted fragment lengths exceed original length when more than one fragment is produced. Identification, source, destination and protocol help associate fragments; offset and MF locate the payload boundaries. If an already fragmented packet is fragmented again, offsets remain relative to the original payload, and a piece that is last only within its parent fragment can still require MF=1. IPv6 routers do not perform the same in-network fragmentation process as IPv4 routers.

examples.prompt: Fragment a 4000-byte datagram with 20-byte header across MTU 1500

steps.title: Separate header from payload
steps.explanation: The original total length includes one header. Headers added to fragments are not part of the original payload offsets.

steps.title: Find the nonfinal capacity
steps.explanation: Each fragment needs its own header and cannot exceed MTU. Nonfinal data sizes must be multiples of eight.

steps.title: Partition and add headers
steps.explanation: The final remainder need not be divisible by eight. Add 20 bytes independently to each payload piece.

steps.title: Calculate offsets and flags
steps.explanation: Offsets count original payload bytes before the fragment in eight-byte units. Only the last fragment has no more fragments after it.

examples.given: IPv4 total length 4000 bytes; fixed 20-byte header without options; MTU 1500.
examples.goal: Calculate every fragment’s total length, offset and MF bit.
examples.strategy: Partition payload only, preserve eight-byte alignment for nonfinal fragments, then restore each header.
examples.verification: Payload sizes sum to 3980 and all fragment lengths are ≤1500. Total transmitted bytes are 4040 because two additional IP headers were introduced.

examples.prompt: Fragment a 1020-byte datagram with header 20 across MTU 620
steps: Original payload=1000; maximum nonfinal payload=600.
Pieces are 600 and 400 bytes.
Offsets are 0 and 75; total fragment lengths are 620 and 420.

pitfalls: Offset units are 8 bytes, not bytes.
Subtract the original header before splitting, then add a header to each fragment.

checks.hint: Offsets use eight-byte units.

checks.prompt: An IP datagram is 2020 bytes with 20-byte header. What is its payload size in bytes?
checks.hint: Remove the header.
checks.explanation: 2020−20=2000 payload bytes.

lessons.title: TCP flow/congestion control, sockets, DNS and HTTP
lessons.intuition: TCP transports an ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission. The receiver’s capacity and the network’s capacity are separate limits. Application protocols then interpret those delivered bytes or use other transport mechanisms.

sections.title: Reliability and windows
sections.body: TCP sequence numbers refer to bytes, and cumulative acknowledgments identify the next expected byte under the usual model. A receive window rwnd advertises buffering capacity. A congestion window cwnd estimates what the sender should inject into the network. The usable limit is approximately min(rwnd,cwnd) minus bytes already outstanding, subject to further implementation rules.

sections.title: Congestion control
sections.body: In the classical teaching model, slow start grows cwnd roughly exponentially per RTT until a threshold or loss indication. Congestion avoidance grows more slowly, often about one MSS per RTT. Timeout and duplicate-ACK loss reactions differ across variants; read the specified algorithm. Bandwidth-delay product estimates data needed in flight to keep a path busy; a too-small window limits throughput.

sections.title: Sockets, DNS and HTTP
sections.body: A TCP server commonly socket/bind/listen/accepts; a client connects, then both send/receive a byte stream without preserved message boundaries. DNS maps names and other records through hierarchy and caches, commonly using UDP but also TCP. HTTP defines methods, status codes, headers and message semantics. Persistent connections reuse transport. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC/UDP, so do not assume every HTTP version uses TCP.

sections.title: Track byte intervals and independent windows
sections.body: A segment with sequence s and b data bytes covers the inclusive byte interval s through s+b−1. If all earlier bytes have arrived, the cumulative ACK is s+b, the next expected byte. Out-of-order arrival need not advance that ACK across a gap. SYN and FIN each consume sequence-number space even without application data. The receive window advertises buffer availability; congestion window is a sender-side network-control quantity. New sending allowance is the smaller window minus bytes already outstanding, bounded below by zero. A large window alone does not guarantee its window/RTT throughput bound is attained: bottleneck link rate, loss, application supply and startup can constrain it further. Retransmission, flow control and congestion control must be tracked as separate mechanisms.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: rwnd=16000 bytes, cwnd=10000 bytes and outstanding=4000. All sizes are in bytes. Outstanding data already consumes window space even if it has not yet been acknowledged.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Limit=\(\min(16000,10000)=10000\). The smaller window governs because satisfying only the larger one can violate receiver or network constraints.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Additional permissible in-flight data is \(10000-4000=6000\) bytes in the simplified model. New data allowance is unused window capacity, not the entire window. A negative result would mean no new data can be sent.

examples.strategy: Apply both window limits, then subtract data already in flight.
examples.answer: Additional permissible in-flight data is \(10000-4000=6000\) bytes in the simplified model.
examples.verification: 4000 outstanding plus 6000 new bytes equals 10000, exactly the congestion limit and within the receiver limit.

steps: A segment starts at sequence 100 and carries 200 bytes.
Those byte numbers are 100 through 299.
If contiguous delivery succeeds, the cumulative ACK is 300, the next expected byte, not 299.

pitfalls: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network.
A TCP read need not correspond to one send call.

checks.prompt: TCP flow control primarily protects which resource?
checks.hint: Compare receive window with congestion window.
checks.explanation: The receiver advertises rwnd to avoid overrunning its capacity. Congestion control addresses network load through cwnd.

checks.prompt: A contiguous segment starts at sequence 500 and carries 100 bytes. What ACK is expected?
checks.hint: ACK the byte after the last delivered byte.
checks.explanation: Bytes 500–599 are delivered, so ACK=600.

The receive window advertises buffer availability; congestion window is a sender-side network-control quantity. New sending allowance is the smaller window minus bytes already outstanding, bounded below by zero. A large window alone does not guarantee its window/RTT throughput bound is attained: bottleneck link rate, loss, application supply and startup can constrain it further. Retransmission, flow control and congestion control must be tracked as separate mechanisms.

method: Mark the first byte number of each segment and the next expected byte in each cumulative acknowledgment.
Compute outstanding bytes and the minimum of congestion and receive windows.
For RTT/throughput problems state whether handshake, slow start, retransmissions, parallelism and serialization are included.

traps.why: It normally identifies the next byte expected; ACK 140 after sequence 100 and 40 payload bytes is consistent.

traps.claim: The advertised receive window is the congestion window
traps.why: Receiver capacity and network congestion are separate constraints; transmission respects both.
