lessons.title: The socket API and TCP byte-stream framing
lessons.intuition: A socket is a programming interface to network communication. Establishing a connection and exchanging application messages are separate tasks. TCP delivers a byte stream, so the application must decide how to recognize message boundaries.

sections.title: Server lifecycle
sections.body: Create a socket, bind it to a local address/port, listen for incoming connections and accept. accept returns a connected socket for one peer while the listening socket remains for future connections. A server can serve multiple clients using threads, processes or nonblocking/event-driven I/O. Privileged-port and address-binding rules depend on the OS.

sections.title: Client and data transfer
sections.body: A TCP client creates a socket and calls connect to the server endpoint. send/recv may transfer fewer bytes than requested; robust code loops as needed. A recv returning zero for a TCP stream indicates an orderly peer closure after available data is exhausted. Errors and timeouts need handling rather than assuming every operation completes immediately.

sections.title: Application framing
sections.body: One send call need not equal one recv call. Define a length prefix, delimiter with escaping, fixed record size or another protocol framing scheme. Accumulate incoming bytes until one complete message is available, retain surplus bytes for the next message, and bound lengths to avoid unbounded allocation. Network byte order converts multibyte integer fields consistently.

sections.title: Message framing over a byte stream
sections.body: TCP supplies reliable ordered bytes but no boundary markers between application writes. A sender can write a length header and payload separately, while a receiver gets a combined chunk, a partial header or a partial payload. A correct receive loop accumulates enough bytes for the agreed header, validates the declared length, then accumulates exactly that many payload bytes. Remaining bytes may belong to the next message and should not be discarded. A return of zero conventionally indicates orderly end of stream, which differs from a short positive read. A listening TCP socket accepts multiple connections into separate connected sockets. UDP preserves datagram boundaries under its API but does not add TCP’s ordered delivery/retransmission guarantees; an application must choose its own reliability semantics.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Encode length 5 in the agreed prefix format. Both peers must agree on prefix size, byte order and length semantics before interpreting payload bytes.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Transmit the prefix and five payload bytes, allowing for partial writes. A short positive write sends only part of the buffer; continue from the first unsent byte rather than retransmitting already sent bytes.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The receiver first accumulates the complete prefix, then exactly five payload bytes, even if several recv calls are needed. The receiver accumulates exactly the declared payload length. A short read does not indicate the message ended.

examples.strategy: Frame the application message independently of TCP send and receive call boundaries.
examples.answer: The receiver first accumulates the complete prefix, then exactly five payload bytes, even if several recv calls are needed.
examples.verification: The reconstructed payload must contain five bytes spelling hello; surplus received bytes may belong to the next framed message.

examples.prompt: A recv returns 3 bytes while 8 remain in the protocol message
steps: Append the 3 bytes to the message buffer.
The remaining expected payload decreases to 5.
Call recv again as necessary; the short read alone is not a protocol failure.

pitfalls: accept returns a new connected socket.
send/recv boundaries are not message boundaries.
revision: Explicit framing and partial-I/O handling belong to the application.

checks.prompt: Does one TCP send call always correspond to exactly one recv call?
checks.hint: TCP can split or combine delivered byte portions.
checks.explanation: Applications need framing and partial-I/O handling because send and recv call boundaries are not preserved as messages.
options: No; TCP preserves bytes, not application message boundaries
Yes if the message is short

checks.prompt: One listening socket accepts 3 connections that remain open. How many socket objects are present, including the listener?
checks.hint: Count the listener plus each accepted socket.
checks.explanation: 1+3=4 sockets.

method: Identify local/remote addresses and ports plus TCP or UDP.

traps.why: TCP preserves ordered bytes, not application message boundaries; framing must be implemented by the application.

lessons.title: DNS hierarchy, resolution and caching
lessons.intuition: DNS distributes naming information across a hierarchy rather than storing every name in one central server. Resolution may require several queries, but caching avoids repeating most of that work until records expire.

sections.title: Names and authority
sections.body: A domain name is a sequence of labels. Root servers direct queries toward relevant top-level-domain servers, which direct them toward authoritative servers for delegated zones. An authoritative answer describes data in that zone; a recursive resolver acts for a client and obtains/caches answers. Delegation boundaries and host labels are not interchangeable concepts.

sections.title: Query behaviour
sections.body: In recursive resolution, the requester asks a resolver to return a final answer or failure. The resolver can use iterative queries, following referrals rather than asking each upstream server to do the whole lookup. Cached records have TTL lifetimes. Caching both answers and referrals can reduce later queries; a cached IP may expire before or after related delegation records.

sections.title: Records and transport
sections.body: A records map names to IPv4 addresses; AAAA to IPv6; CNAME expresses aliases; MX identifies mail exchangers; NS identifies name servers. DNS commonly uses UDP port 53 for ordinary queries and can use TCP, including for larger/truncated responses and zone transfers under their relevant rules. DNS is not always UDP, and a domain can map to more than one address.

sections.title: Delegation and caches change the query path
sections.body: The root directs a resolver toward a top-level-domain authority, which can direct it toward an authoritative server for a narrower zone. These are referrals, not necessarily the final host address. A recursive resolver performs this work on behalf of its client; iterative exchanges supply answers or referrals one step at a time. Cached answers and delegation records have separate TTLs, so a cache can skip some exchanges but still need an authoritative lookup. A CNAME is an alias whose target may require further resolution; MX selects mail-exchanger names, not automatically their numeric IP addresses. Delay counting should identify which requests are serial and which cached records exist at the start. UDP is common for queries, but TCP and other DNS transports also exist; protocol correctness is not equivalent to a single UDP exchange.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: A client asks its recursive resolver. The stub asks for recursive service; it need not itself contact every level of the hierarchy.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: The resolver follows root and TLD referrals to a relevant authoritative server. Root and TLD typically return delegation information, not the final address for the requested host.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: It returns the answer and caches permitted records for their TTLs; future queries can skip steps if caches are valid. Caching changes later paths and delay counts; TTL constrains reuse instead of making an answer permanent.

examples.strategy: Follow referrals until the appropriate authoritative answer is obtained.
examples.answer: It returns the answer and caches permitted records for their TTLs; future queries can skip steps if caches are valid.
examples.verification: Confirm the final answer is authoritative for the requested name or follow its alias; do not treat a referral as the host-address answer.

examples.prompt: A cached record has TTL 120 seconds and was stored 45 seconds ago
steps: Assuming no refresh or eviction, remaining valid lifetime is 75 seconds.
A query before expiry can use the cached record.
After expiry, the resolver must obtain fresh information rather than trusting that TTL indefinitely.

pitfalls: Recursive resolver and authoritative server have different roles.
DNS also uses TCP.

checks.prompt: TTL was 180 seconds and 70 seconds have elapsed. What is remaining lifetime?
checks.hint: Subtract elapsed time.

checks.prompt: How many bits are in the address returned by an IPv4 A record?
checks.hint: Use IPv4 address width.
checks.explanation: IPv4 addresses contain 32 bits.

Apply available cached records before counting queries and delays.

traps.claim: Every lookup must contact the root server
traps.why: Cached delegations and answers can skip most resolution steps.

lessons.title: HTTP requests, responses and persistent connections
lessons.intuition: HTTP defines application-level meaning: which resource is requested, what action is asked for and how the response is described. Its semantics are separate from the transport connection and remain recognizable across protocol versions.

sections.title: Request and response structure
sections.body: A request carries a method, target and headers, often with a body. GET retrieves a representation; POST commonly submits processing data; PUT replaces at a known target under its semantics. A response includes a status code, headers and possibly a body. Status classes 2xx indicate success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client-side request problems and 5xx server-side failures.

sections.title: Persistence and latency
sections.body: Persistent connections reuse transport for multiple requests, reducing repeated setup. HTTP/1.1 generally supports persistent connections; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams within its transport model. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than TCP. A latency question must specify DNS/cache state, connection establishment, transfer size, request dependencies and whether connections can be reused.

sections.title: Caching and security
sections.body: Cache-Control and related metadata control reuse; conditional requests can validate existing content rather than redownload it. HTTPS protects HTTP exchange using the applicable secure transport, but does not change what GET or a status code means. An HTTP cache and a DNS cache store different information and can have unrelated expiry times.

sections.title: Build an explicit latency model
sections.body: For one object over a fresh TCP connection, a simplified model counts one RTT for establishment and one RTT for the request and start of response, then object transmission. It omits DNS, TLS, congestion startup and queuing unless supplied. Persistence reuses the connection and avoids repeating setup. HTTP/1.1 without pipelining can still issue requests sequentially; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a connection; HTTP/3 uses QUIC streams over UDP. Cache freshness can avoid a network request, while conditional validation still contacts the server and may receive 304 rather than a complete body. An HTTP error status is a valid application response; connection refusal occurs before such a response. Any numerical RTT answer must specify connection reuse, parallel connections and which transfers overlap.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The server produced a valid protocol response. Receiving an HTTP status line implies that an application-level response was exchanged over an established transport.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Its status is in the 4xx category and indicates the requested resource was not found under the response semantics. 404 concerns the requested resource, not the inability to contact the server at all.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: This is not the same as a TCP connection refusal, where no HTTP exchange may have occurred. Connection refusal prevents the request/response exchange; retrying it is a different diagnostic path from inspecting a 404 URL.

examples.strategy: Distinguish a completed HTTP exchange with an error status from a failed transport connection.
examples.answer: This is not the same as a TCP connection refusal, where no HTTP exchange may have occurred.
examples.verification: A response status and body can be displayed for HTTP 404. With connection refusal there may be no HTTP response to parse.

examples.prompt: Compare three requests with/without transport reuse
steps: If each new TCP connection costs one setup RTT, three separate connections pay three setup RTTs in this simplified model.
One persistent connection pays one setup RTT.
Two setup RTTs are saved; actual response delays and transfers must still be included.

pitfalls: Connection refusal is not an HTTP error response.
HTTP/3 does not use TCP.
revision: 2xx success; 3xx redirect; 4xx request issue; 5xx server failure.

checks.prompt: What is the hundred-class digit of HTTP status 503?
checks.hint: Divide into the status family.
checks.explanation: 503 belongs to 5xx, whose class digit is 5.

checks.prompt: Three separate one-RTT setups are replaced by one reused connection. How many setup RTTs are saved?
checks.hint: Compare three with one.
checks.explanation: 3−1=2 setup RTTs saved under the stated model.

traps.why: Without pipelining or multiplexing, requests can remain sequential on one connection.

traps.claim: All HTTP uses TCP

name: General Aptitude
description: Extra exam practice beyond your CS PDF

lessons.title: Quantitative aptitude: ratios, percentages and work
lessons.intuition: Quantitative aptitude usually rewards a clean model rather than lengthy computation. Define units and the reference quantity first. A percentage is relative to a base; a work time converts to a rate before people working together can be combined.

sections.title: Ratios and averages
sections.body: If A:B=a:b, write A=ak and B=bk. This preserves the relationship while totals determine k. A weighted average is total weighted value divided by total weight, not the unweighted average of subgroup averages. Check whether group sizes are equal before averaging percentages.

sections.title: Successive changes
sections.body: Increase by p% multiplies by 1+p/100; decrease by q% multiplies by 1−q/100. Combine multipliers to find overall change. Equal percentage rises and falls do not cancel because their bases differ. Profit percentage uses cost price as its base unless explicitly redefined.

sections.title: Work and speed
sections.body: A worker completing one job in t days works at 1/t jobs per day under constant-rate assumptions. Independent rates add for shared work; time is reciprocal total rate. Distance=rate×time with consistent units. Relative speed adds for opposite travel directions and subtracts for same-direction catch-up.

steps.title: Apply the increase
steps.explanation: The first percentage has base 100.

steps.title: Apply the decrease to its actual base
steps.explanation: The second percentage has base 120. Its absolute decrease is 24, larger than the original increase 20.

steps.title: Measure change relative to the original
steps.explanation: Net percentage must use the initial value as denominator, not 120 or 96.

examples.given: Initial value 100; a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease.
examples.goal: Find final value and net percentage change.
examples.strategy: Apply each percentage to its current base, using multiplication rather than subtracting percentages.
examples.answer: Final value 96; overall decrease 4%.
examples.verification: For equal fractional increase/decrease r, (1+r)(1−r)=1−r². With r=0.2, the loss is 0.04=4%.

examples.prompt: A finishes in 6 days and B in 3 days
steps: Rates are 1/6 and 1/3 jobs/day.
Combined rate=1/2 job/day.
Time for one job=\(\frac1{1/2}=2\) days under constant independent rates.

pitfalls: Percentages of different bases cannot be simply added.
Add work rates, not completion times.

checks.prompt: A price of 200 rises by 15%. What is its new price?
checks.hint: Multiply by 1.15.

checks.prompt: Two workers each finish a job in 8 days. Together how many days do they need?
checks.hint: Add their equal rates.
checks.explanation: 1/8+1/8=1/4 job/day, so 4 days.

method: Define unknowns, units and the base quantity for each percentage.
Convert the wording into an equation and solve before evaluating options.
Check boundary cases and approximate magnitude; use substitution into the original condition to reject plausible-looking distractors.

traps.why: Starting at 100, +20% gives 120 and −20% gives 96; the second base has changed.

traps.why: For equal distances the harmonic mean applies because travel times differ.

Constant independent work rates combined on the same job.

lessons.title: Verbal, analytical and spatial aptitude
lessons.prerequisite: Reading comprehension and careful constraint tracking.
lessons.intuition: Reasoning tasks ask you to respect exactly the available evidence. In verbal problems, grammatical role and meaning constrain the answer; in arrangements, each clue reduces the allowed states. Spatial questions require tracking invariants through transformations rather than guessing from familiarity.

sections.title: Language and comprehension
sections.body: For grammar, identify subject, verb, modifiers and required agreement. Distinguish possession (their), contraction (they’re) and location (there). For passages, separate explicit statements from reasonable but unsupported assumptions. An inference must follow from the passage, not merely be plausible in real life. Analogy questions should preserve the exact relationship, such as increasing intensity or part-to-whole.

sections.title: Analytical constraints
sections.body: Translate clues into explicit relations: before, immediately before, adjacent or not adjacent are different. Draw positions, place fixed clues, then enumerate remaining possibilities systematically. In circular seating, rotationally equivalent arrangements may be treated as the same, but reflection equivalence depends on the question. Use a counterexample arrangement to test whether a claim must always hold.

sections.title: Spatial transformations
sections.body: A rotation preserves orientation/chirality and pairwise distances; a reflection reverses handedness. For cube nets, track which faces become opposite, then rule out options placing opposite faces adjacent. When counting figures, classify by size and position so overlaps are included without counting the same figure twice. Explicit sketches are useful working tools.

examples.prompt: Three positions with A immediately before B and C after B

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: A,B must occupy adjacent positions in that order. The pair can start only at position 1 or 2 in a three-position arrangement.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: C must lie to their right, so A,B cannot occupy positions 2,3. If the pair occupies 2,3 there is no position right of B for C. This eliminates that case rather than merely making it unlikely.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Only A,B,C remains. Replacing “immediately” with “somewhere” would weaken the adjacency requirement. The surviving arrangement satisfies both adjacency and the after-B condition.

examples.strategy: Translate “immediately before” into an adjacent ordered pair and apply the remaining position constraint.
examples.answer: Only A,B,C remains. Replacing “immediately” with “somewhere” would weaken the adjacency requirement.
examples.verification: In A,B,C, B follows A immediately and C is right of B. All three positions are filled exactly once.

steps: The noun books needs a possessive determiner.
Their means belonging to them; they’re expands to they are and cannot fill that noun-modifying role.
There describes location. Choose using grammatical function, not sound.

pitfalls: Do not add unstated constraints.
Immediately before differs from before.
A mirror image need not be obtainable by rotation.

checks.hint: Try every location for the A,B pair.
checks.explanation: Only A,B,C satisfies both constraints.

checks.prompt: Four distinct people stand in a line without restrictions. How many arrangements are possible?
checks.hint: Use factorial ordering.

traps.why: The passage may not support it; the answer must follow from the given text.

traps.why: These quantifiers express different strengths; strengthening a statement can turn a valid inference into an unsupported one.
